title: Longest consecutive sequence in O(n) — how do you avoid sorting?
front: Longest consecutive sequence in O(n) — how do you avoid sorting?
back:
Put everything in a set for O(1) membership, then for each number ask "am I the start of a run?" — you are iff `num - 1` not in the set. Only then walk upward counting `num + 1, num + 2, …`.
Why it's O(n) despite the nested loop: the inner walk only runs for numbers that begin a run, so each run is traversed exactly once — total work is bounded (same amortised argument as the monotonic stack).
The set is for membership, not traversal. Reaching for `nums_set[0]` is the signal you're still thinking in order.

front: BST — how do you find the lowest common ancestor of p and q, and why does it work?
back: Walk from the root: both values smaller than curr → go left · both larger → go right · otherwise (they split, or one equals curr) → curr is the LCA. Works because a BST guarantees left < node < right, so the first place p and q diverge is the deepest node containing both. O(h) time, O(1) space iteratively.

Branch.lend_books(10)

Hardcoding works until someone subclasses. Also: a static method that reaches for `MyClass.something` should probably have been a classmethod.

title: Size-k heap — how do you decide min-heap or max-heap? Why does it read
front: Size-k heap — how do you decide min-heap or max-heap? Why does it read backwards?
back:
Ask which element should leave when the heap overflows — that one must sit at `heap[0]`. The heap holds your worst survivor on top, ready to evict, not your best.
keep the k LARGEST → evict the smallest → MIN-heap → no negation (LC215, 703)
keep the k SMALLEST → evict the largest → MAX-heap → negate (LC973)
Counterintuitive because keeping the largest uses a min-heap. The heap is a rejection mechanism, not a collection.

Seed `{0:1}` = the empty prefix before any elements; without it, subarrays starting at index 0 are never counted.

title: Floyd's cycle detection — the two phases, and why is the meeting point
front: Floyd's cycle detection — the two phases, and why is the meeting point not the answer?
back:
Phase 1 slow = nums[slow] (×1)
 fast = nums[nums[fast]] (×2)
 until slow == fast → you're somewhere INSIDE the loop
Phase 2 reset slow2 = start; move BOTH ×1
 until slow == slow2 → that point IS the cycle entrance
Phase 1 only proves a cycle exists — they meet at an arbitrary point in it, not the entrance. Phase 2 works because fast travelled exactly twice slow's distance, so the distance from the meeting point around to the entrance equals the distance from the start to the entrance. Equal-speed pointers from those two places arrive together. O(n) time, O(1) space.

title: You need to deep-copy a structure whose nodes point at each other (lin
front: You need to deep-copy a structure whose nodes point at each other (linked list with random pointers, a graph). What's the pattern?
back: Build a translation dict `{original: copy}` in a first pass — create the copies, wire nothing. Then in a second pass, translate every pointer through the map: `copy.next = map[curr.next]`, `copy.random = map[curr.random]`. Key insight: all pointer fields are the same operation — "turn an original reference into its copy" — so treat structural (`next`) and non-structural (`random`) links identically. Node objects work as dict keys (hashed by identity).

title: A class attribute counting something about instances (`active_devices`
front: A class attribute counting something about instances (`active_devices`, `total_balance`). What silently goes wrong?
back: It's a snapshot, not a live value — nothing keeps it in sync after construction. `alice.balance = 5000` leaves `total_balance` stale; `turn_on()` called twice double-counts one device. Two fixes: update on every change (every code path must remember, and one that forgets corrupts it silently), or compute on demand from the instances (can't drift, costs a walk). General: stored derived values drift from what they're derived from.

title: How do you heap things by a key that isn't the value itself?

title: Monotonic deque for a sliding window — why store indices, and what's t
front: Monotonic deque for a sliding window — why store indices, and what's the expiry check?
back: You can't test a value for whether it's still in the window — only a position can be compared to the window bounds. With the window ending at `i` and size `k`, the valid range is `[i-k+1, i]`, so the front has expired when `dq[0] <= i - k`. Also: only start recording once the first window is full (`i >= k - 1`).

title: Python — when can you turn a recursion into a plain loop?
front: Python — when can you turn a recursion into a plain loop?
back: When the recursive call is the last thing you do and you pass its result straight up unchanged (`return self.f(child, ...)` with no further work) — that's tail recursion. Replace the call with "move the pointer" and wrap in `while`. Saves the call stack: O(h) space → O(1). Doesn't apply when you combine child results (`1 + max(L, R)`) — that needs the stack.

title: Topological sort via DFS — where does the append go, and why?
front: Topological sort via DFS — where does the append go, and why?
back:
After the loop over the node's dependencies. A node joins the list only once everything it depends on is already there — that's a post-order append, and it's what makes the result a valid ordering with no sorting step.
for pre in graph[node]: dfs(pre)
completed.add(node)
res.append(node) # ← only now
Same shape as measuring-mode tree recursion: handle the children, then act on yourself.
Watch the edge direction: graph mapping node → dependencies gives the order forward. Mapping node → dependents gives it reversed, needing `res[::-1]`.

Replace (no super) — the child's behaviour is entirely different: `FlightHero.use_power` returns a flying message, nothing of the parent's applies. Extend (call super) — you want the parent's work plus something:
def attack(self):
 super().attack() # parent's behaviour
 print(f"For the {self.team}!") # plus the child's
An override that only calls `super()` and adds nothing is redundant — delete it.

title: Evaluating RPN with a stack — what's the trap on `-` and `/`?
front: Evaluating RPN with a stack — what's the trap on `-` and `/`?
back: The first value popped is the RIGHT operand. So `b = pop(); a = pop()` then `a - b`, `a / b`. Reversed, `+` and `*` still pass (commutative) and only `-` and `/` break — so a wrong version looks half-correct. Also: use `int(a / b)` for truncation toward zero, not `//` which floors toward −∞ (`7 // -3 = -3` vs `int(7/-3) = -2`).

title: Write the grid DFS skeleton. What three rejections go in the guard?
front: Write the grid DFS skeleton. What three rejections go in the guard?
back:
rows, cols = len(grid), len(grid[0]) # hoist — don't recompute per call
visited = set()
def dfs(r, c):
 if r < 0 or c < 0 or r == rows or c == cols \
 or grid[r][c] == "0" or (r, c) in visited:
 return
 visited.add((r, c))
 dfs(r+1, c); dfs(r-1, c); dfs(r, c+1); dfs(r, c-1)
Out of bounds (both directions, both axes) · wrong cell type · already visited. Guard first, mark only if it passes — a bare `return` exits immediately, so rejected cells never enter `visited`.

title: What does MRO stand for, and what does it determine?
front: What does MRO stand for, and what does it determine?
back: Method Resolution Order — the sequence Python searches for an attribute or method, taking the first match. Inspect it with `Cls.__mro__`. Ordered left to right across parents: `class D(B, C)` → `(D, B, C, A, object)`. Each class appears exactly once, a class always precedes its parents, and `object` ends every chain. title: "Which edge creates the cycle?" — why is extracting the cycle from a f

Extracting the cycle properly needs a path stack with push/pop. Build the graph incrementally instead: before adding each edge, check whether its endpoints are already connected. The first one that is, is the answer — and "last in input" falls out for free because you process in order.

title: Contiguous-subarray-sums-to-k. Why is sliding window wrong, and what's
front: Contiguous-subarray-sums-to-k. Why is sliding window wrong, and what's the tell?
back: A window assumes monotonicity — adding grows the sum, removing shrinks it — so "too big → shrink" makes progress. Negatives break that: shrinking might raise the sum, so the pointer has no rule. `[1,-1,1], k=1` has 3 answers; a window finds 2. title: You need `getMin()` (or max) in O(1) alongside normal stack operations
front: You need `getMin()` (or max) in O(1) alongside normal stack operations. What's the trick?
back: A second stack of minimums, maintained in parallel. `getMin` is then just `min_stack[-1]`. Two valid designs: (a) push a running min on every push → both stacks stay equal length, `pop` pops both unconditionally (more space, simpler). (b) push only when `val <= current min`, and pop `min_stack` only when `stack[-1] == min_stack[-1]` (less space, `pop` needs a comparison). General idea: you can't compute it fast later, so record it as you go.

title: Brute force scans forward from each element to find the next greater.
front: Brute force scans forward from each element to find the next greater. What does the stack version do instead?
back: It inverts the direction. Brute force asks, per element, "scanning ahead, who beats me?" — re-examining the same elements repeatedly. The stack asks, at each new element, "who's been waiting that I beat?" — looking backward at the waiting list. That inversion is what turns O(n²) into O(n): each element is examined once when pushed, once when popped.

title: How do you find the median of a growing stream in O(1), when a heap on
front: How do you find the median of a growing stream in O(1), when a heap only gives you one extreme?
back: Split the data in half and make the middle into two extremes. A max-heap for the lower half (negated, since Python has no max-heap) and a min-heap for the upper half. The median sits at their tops: the largest of the small half and the smallest of the large half — both O(1) to read. Odd count → the top of whichever heap is bigger. title: Write the monotonic stack skeleton, and say what the stack holds.
front: Write the monotonic stack skeleton, and say what the stack holds.
back:
res = [default] * len(nums) # pre-fill: never-popped items keep the default
stack = [] # items STILL WAITING; values decrease bottom→top
for i, x in enumerate(nums):
 while stack and nums[stack[-1]] < x: # x beats the top
 j = stack.pop()
 res[j] = <answer for j> # x IS j's answer
 stack.append(i)
Decreasing order is automatic — anything beaten has already been popped. Leftovers at the end never found a bigger element, so the pre-filled default (0 or -1) handles them with no cleanup loop.

title: Serialising a list of strings where any character could appear in the

back: Length-prefix each item: `f"{len(s)}#{s}"`. On decode, read the length first, then take exactly that many characters — the content is never scanned for delimiters, so nothing needs escaping. The caller writes plain attribute syntax while your code still runs validation:

The payoff: you can ship a public attribute and add validation later without changing any calling code. That's why Python doesn't need getters everywhere the way Java does.

Back (same as the stack): pop anything smaller than the incoming element — it's dominated, since the newcomer is bigger and stays in the window longer.
Front: the head is the current max, but it may have expired — slid out of the window — so evict it by index. Stacks have no expiry; windows do. That's the whole difference.

(2) Leftovers at the end — an unclosed `"("` leaves the stack non-empty, so the final check is usually `return not stack`. Push-only problems fail silently without it.

1. Unvisited: Node has not been encountered yet.
2. Visiting (Active Path): Node is currently on the active recursion stack. Re-encountering a node in this state = CYCLE DETECTED.
3. Visited (Completed): Node and all its dependencies are fully processed and added to the result. Safe to return True immediately.

title: BFS counting levels/minutes — why does a naive `level += 1` per iterat

back:
The final level pops the last wave and produces nothing — a real iteration, but not elapsed time. Fix: only count a level that actually did something:
while queue:
 for _ in range(len(queue)):
 ...
 if queue: # something was pushed → a unit passed

Check three cases: one source + one target → 1 · nothing to do → 0 · no sources at all → 0.

Then `defaultdict(list)` + append, and return `list(d.values())`. The whole trick is choosing a key that collapses the equivalence class.

title: You have three possible outcomes but wrote `if A and B: ... else: ...`
front: You have three possible outcomes but wrote `if A and B: ... else: ...`. What breaks?
back: A flat if/else gives only two branches, so two of your three cases collapse into the `else`. In 523: not seen → store · seen, gap ok → True · seen, gap too small → do nothing — that third case wrongly falls into the else and overwrites the stored index. Fix: nest, or invert the guard (`if run not in seen: store` / `elif gap >= 2: return True`). Ask how many distinct behaviours you need before choosing the branch shape.

back: `-2`. `//` floors toward negative infinity, not toward zero. -3/2 = -1.5, and "down" from -1.5 is -2. Note `int()` disagrees: `int(-1.5)` = -1 (truncates toward zero). On negatives, `//` and `int()` give different answers.

title: What does polymorphism let you avoid writing?
front: What does polymorphism let you avoid writing?
back:
Type-branching. Without it, every new type means editing the caller:
if isinstance(thing, Dog): print("Woof")
elif isinstance(thing, Cat): print("Meow") # add a Cow? edit this.
With it, the caller is one line — `thing.speak()` — and Python resolves to the right version at runtime, based on the actual object. Behaviour lives with the type instead of in a branching function, so adding a new type touches nothing that already exists.

title: `heapq.heapify(lst)` — what does it do, and when do you use it instead
front: `heapq.heapify(lst)` — what does it do, and when do you use it instead of pushing?
back: Turns an existing list into a heap in place, in O(n) — beats n pushes at O(n log n). Returns `None` (a mutator). Use it when you have all the data up front; use `heappush` when items arrive one at a time. Gotcha: a heapified list is not sorted — only `lst[0]` is guaranteed. `[5,1,9,3,7]` heapifies to `[1,3,9,5,7]`.

front: Python — when a function should return True/False based on a condition, what should you write?
back: Return the condition directly. `return a and b`, `return a or b`, `return x and not y`. Never `return True if cond else False` — the condition is already a boolean. Also skip `if x == True` → just `if x`.

front: BFS where several things spread simultaneously (rotting oranges, fire, infection). What changes?
back: Seed the queue with every starting point up front, not one. The level loop is unchanged — each level is one unit of time, and all sources advance in lockstep automatically. No special handling; the queue does it.

title: `return stones[0] or 0` — why doesn't this protect against an empty li
front: `return stones[0] or 0` — why doesn't this protect against an empty list?
back: The indexing happens first — `stones[0]` raises IndexError before `or` is ever evaluated. `or` can only pick between values that already exist. Use `stones[0] if stones else 0`. Second problem: if `stones[0]` is legitimately `0` (falsy), `or` skips it — same trap as `prefix[i] or postfix[i+1]`. `or` is not a null-check.

front: Tree recursion — what does `if not node: return X` actually do, and how do you pick X?
back: It fires when you step past a leaf into `None` — that's the floor that stops the recursion and starts the unwind. X is the neutral value for what you're computing: 0 for depth/sum/count, `True` for "is it balanced", `float('inf')` for a min you want ignored. Ask: what should a nonexistent subtree contribute?

It raises a ValueError because iterating directly over a dictionary yields only keys (strings/ints), not key-value tuples. You must use 'for k, v in my_dict.items():'.

title: Monotonic stack has a `while` nested inside a `for`. Why is it O(n), n
front: Monotonic stack has a `while` nested inside a `for`. Why is it O(n), not O(n²)?
back: Each index is pushed exactly once and popped at most once, so across the entire run there are at most n pops — not n pops per iteration. Some iterations pop five things, most pop zero; the total is bounded by the number of pushes. n pushes + ≤n pops = O(n). The argument: count total work across the whole run, not per iteration. Same reason the monotonic deque in Sliding Window Maximum is O(n).

title: Directed-graph cycle detection — why isn't one `visited` set enough?
front: Directed-graph cycle detection — why isn't one `visited` set enough?
back:
Revisiting a node isn't automatically a cycle — you can legitimately reach it via two different paths. A cycle is reaching a node currently on the path you're walking. So you need two markers:
path set — add BEFORE recursing, REMOVE after → "am I inside this right now?"
done/memo — set once, never cleared → "already proven fine"
Grid problems only ever needed the second. Missing the path set means no cycle detection; missing the memo means re-walking subtrees and exponential blowup.

title: Prefix sum — when do you store a COUNT vs an INDEX, and how does the s
front: Prefix sum — when do you store a COUNT vs an INDEX, and how does the seed change?
back: Counting subarrays → `prefix → count`, seed `{0: 1}`, always update. Length/position questions → `prefix → FIRST index`, seed `{0: -1}`, never overwrite (a later index shrinks the gap and can fail a length test). For divisibility, store `run % k` instead of `run` — two equal remainders mean the stretch between them is divisible by k.

title: Queue vs stack — what's the difference, and which traversal does each
front: Queue vs stack — what's the difference, and which traversal does each produce?
back: Queue = FIFO (a line) → `deque`, `popleft()` → BFS, level by level. Stack = LIFO (a pile) → `list`, `pop()` → DFS, dive deep first. Why: with a queue, children go behind everyone at the current depth, so a level finishes before the next starts. Recursion is implicitly a stack — which is why a recursive solution gives you depth-first order, not level order.

title: Python — instance method vs `@classmethod` vs `@staticmethod`. How do
front: Python — instance method vs `@classmethod` vs `@staticmethod`. How do you choose?
back:
Ask what it needs:
needs THIS OBJECT's data → def m(self) instance method
needs THE CLASS's data → @classmethod, def m(cls)
needs NEITHER → @staticmethod, def m()
`cls` is to the class what `self` is to the instance — the thing passed in automatically. A method with an unused `self` is a signal the decorator is missing (linters flag it).

title: Four ways to build a frequency dict — which and when?
front: Four ways to build a frequency dict — which and when?
back:
if x in d: d[x] += 1 # manual, verbose
else: d[x] = 1
d[x] = d.get(x, 0) + 1 # plain dict, one line
d = defaultdict(int); d[x] += 1 # no branch at all
Counter(items) # one call, plus .most_common(k)
`Counter` is the default unless you need something it doesn't do. `defaultdict(int)` when you're accumulating something other than a plain count.

title: What's wrong with `try: ... except: pass`?
front: What's wrong with `try: ... except: pass`?
back:
It catches everything — including genuine bugs like a `TypeError` from a typo, or a `NameError` — and silently carries on. It turns crashes into wrong answers, which are much harder to find. In Baseball Game it hid a branching bug: `'C'` was falling into the number branch, `float('C')` failed, and the `except` swallowed it.
Rules: catch the specific error (`except ValueError:`), never `pass` silently unless you genuinely mean "ignore this case", and don't reach for `try` at all when the code's structure already guarantees the input is valid.

Then think about only one level: given those two answers, how do I produce mine? E.g. depth: "left is 3 deep, right is 5 deep → I'm `1 + max(3,5)`." The stack handles everything below.

title: Remove duplicates from a sorted array in place, keeping at most k copi
front: Remove duplicates from a sorted array in place, keeping at most k copies — write the loop, and say what `l` means.
back:
l = 0 # l = COUNT of kept elements, not an index
for r in range(len(nums)):
 if l < k or nums[r] != nums[l - k]:

back: When it must persist across all calls. A plain local is created fresh on every call and dies when that call returns — so a running max/counter resets constantly. `self.x` lives on the object, so every recursive call sees and updates the same one. Pattern: outer method sets `self.best = 0`, helper updates `self.best`, outer returns it.

title: Python — `name`, `_name`, `__name`: what's the difference?
front: Python — `name`, `_name`, `__name`: what's the difference?
back: `name` public — the default; everything in Python is public unless marked. `_name` protected — pure convention, meaning "internal, don't touch." Nothing enforces it. `__name` private — triggers name mangling: Python renames it to `_ClassName__name`, so `obj.__name` from outside raises AttributeError. title: Python — how do you know whether a list/dict/set method returns someth
front: Python — how do you know whether a list/dict/set method returns something useful or `None`?
back:
Ask: am I asking the object something, or telling it to change?
• QUERY (object unchanged) → returns the answer: `.index(x)` · `.count(x)` · `len(lst)` · `x in lst`
• MUTATOR (changes the object) → returns `None`: `.append` · `.extend` · `.insert` · `.remove` · `.clear` · `.sort` · `.reverse` · `.update` · `.add`
• Odd one out: `.pop(i)` mutates AND returns the removed item (that info would otherwise be lost).
So: `return queue.index(name)` ✓ · `return queue.append(name)` ✗ (returns None — append on one line, return the list on the next).

title: Two-heap median — why isn't it enough to push each number onto whichev
front: Two-heap median — why isn't it enough to push each number onto whichever heap is smaller?
back:
That splits by arrival order, not by value — a small number can land in the "high" half purely because it arrived when that heap was short. Every number must take the same path:
heappush(low, -num) # always into low
heappush(high, -heappop(low)) # move low's MAX across ← this sorts them
if len(high) > len(low): # rebalance sizes
 heappush(low, -heappop(high))
The cross-push is what compares the new value against the existing partition. No branching at entry.

 dfs(r, c) # swallow it so its other cells don't re-trigger
Separation: dfs explores, the loop counts.

PRE-ORDER (pass down) act on node; dfs(left, ctx); dfs(right, ctx)

title: How many nodes does a perfect binary tree of depth `d` have, and why?

back: `2**d - 1`. Levels double: 1, 2, 4, 8 — every node has exactly two children. Totals are 1, 3, 7, 15, each one less than a power of two. (Powers of two, not factorials — factorials multiply by an increasing number.) Useful as a definitional test: a subtree is perfect iff `size == 2**depth - 1`, which beats any proxy check.

title: A grid guard that compares against a fixed value (`== "1"`, `!= INF`)
front: A grid guard that compares against a fixed value (`== "1"`, `!= INF`) vs one that compares against where you came from. What changes?
back:
The previous cell's value has to arrive as a parameter — the pass-down pattern:
def dfs(r, c, visited, prev_height):
 if ... or heights[r][c] > prev_height: # can't flow uphill
 return
 dfs(r+1, c, visited, heights[r][c]) # pass MY height down
Seed with the cell's own height so the first check passes. And note reversing the search flips the comparison: walking downhill from a cell uses `>`, walking uphill from an ocean uses `<`.

title: Counting connected shapes in a grid — when can you skip DFS entirely?
front: Counting connected shapes in a grid — when can you skip DFS entirely?
back:
When the constraints guarantee each shape has one identifiable anchor cell. Battleships are straight lines with gaps between them, so every ship has exactly one top-left cell — count an `X` only if there's no `X` above it and none to its left:
if board[r][c] == "X" and (r == 0 or board[r-1][c] == ".") \
 and (c == 0 or board[r][c-1] == "."):
 count += 1
O(1) space, no visited set. Only valid under those constraints — DFS is the general answer and survives shapes that bend. General move: when the shapes are constrained, count anchors instead of traversing.

back: It's plain binary search on the API's answer. -1 (guess too high) → search lower → `r = mid - 1`. 1 (too low) → search higher → `l = mid + 1`. 0 → return mid. title: What kind of problem is a stack problem?
front: What kind of problem is a stack problem?
back:
Anything about deferred work you must return to in reverse order of arrival — LIFO. Tells: "matching"/"nesting" (parentheses, HTML tags), "most recent" (undo, back button), "pending operands" (RPN — number → push, operator → pop two, apply, push result). title: `super()` — what does it mean, and what's the shape of using it in `__
front: `super()` — what does it mean, and what's the shape of using it in `__init__`?
back:
"The next class's version of this method." Standard pattern — parent does its share, child adds its own:
def __init__(self, name, power, team):
 super().__init__(name, power) # only what the PARENT expects
 self.team = team # the child's addition
Two stumbles: `super()` takes no arguments, and you pass no `self` — `super().attack()`, not `super().attack(self)`. And the parent's `__init__` does not run automatically once you define your own.

title: List vs tuple?
front: List vs tuple?
back: List is mutable (append, change, remove), tuple is immutable. Tuples are hashable, so usable as dict keys and set elements. Use tuples for fixed records (`(lat, lon)`), lists for collections that change.

title: Tree path problems — why can't you track "what I've seen so far" in a
front: Tree path problems — why can't you track "what I've seen so far" in a shared list/queue?
back: A shared structure accumulates across sibling branches, not just ancestors. After finishing a left subtree its values are still in there when you enter the right one — but they aren't on that path. You'd have to pop exactly on the way out (backtracking). A parameter avoids all of it: the call stack IS the path. Each frame holds its own copy; unwinding discards it automatically.

title: Python — what is `self`, mechanically?
front: Python — what is `self`, mechanically?
back: Just a parameter — the first one every method gets, holding the object it was called on. `a.speak()` is really `Dog.speak(a)`; Python slides the thing before the dot into the first slot. That's how one shared method knows which object's data to touch. The name is convention only — `def speak(banana)` works identically.

title: `self.followers = {}` vs `defaultdict(set)` — what does the defaultdic
front: `self.followers = {}` vs `defaultdict(set)` — what does the defaultdict buy you?
back:
With a plain dict, reaching into a missing key raises KeyError — so every access needs a guard first:
if uid not in self.followers:
 self.followers[uid] = set()
self.followers[uid].add(x)
`defaultdict(set)` manufactures an empty set on first access, so it's one line:
self.followers[uid].add(x)
The two-step nature is why the guard is needed at all: `d[k].add(x)` means look up the value, then act on it — step one fails before `.add` is ever reached. `defaultdict` makes step one always succeed. Use `defaultdict(list)` for appending, `defaultdict(int)` for counters (`d[k] += 1`).
Side effect: merely reading `d[k]` creates the entry. So `unfollow` on a user who never followed anyone leaves an empty set behind — harmless, but surprising if you later iterate the keys or check `len(d)`.

title: Python — what do `word[-5]`, `word[-5:]`, and `word[:-5]` each give yo

back:
For `word = 'heaviness'`:
- `word[-5]` → `'i'` — ONE character (index, no colon), 5th from the end
- `word[-5:]` → `'iness'` — the LAST FIVE (colon AFTER the number = keep from there on)
- `word[:-5]` → `'heavi'` — all EXCEPT the last five (colon BEFORE = stop there)
The last two are complementary halves: `word[:-n] + word[-n:] == word`
Mnemonic: colon after → KEEP the tail · colon before → DROP the tail.
`word[-5]` = ONE character, the 5th from the end. `word[-5:]` = the LAST FIVE characters (slice). To drop the last n: `word[:-n]`. So: `'heaviness'[-5]` → `'i'`; `'heaviness'[-5:]` → `'iness'`; `'heaviness'[:-5]` → `'heavi'`. The colon makes it a range.

title: You're storing tweets. Key by `tweetId` or by `userId`?

title: Tree min depth — why does `1 + min(L, R)` fail, when `1 + max(L, R)` w

back: A missing child returns 0. `max` ignores the 0 (the real subtree wins), but `min` prefers it — so a node with one child reports depth 1 instead of walking down the real side. Min depth means "to a leaf" (a node with no children); `None` isn't a leaf. Fix: handle the one-child case explicitly, or return infinity for a missing child so `min` never picks it.

title: Prefix sum + hashmap — what's the algebra that turns "subarray sums to

So at each position, keeping a running sum, ask: "have I already passed a prefix equal to `run - k`?" Each earlier match marks the start of a subarray ending here. It's a lookup, not a search.

title: BFS on a tree — you know the level-order loop. How much changes for ri
front: BFS on a tree — you know the level-order loop. How much changes for right side view, level averages, or max per level?
back:
Only the extraction line. Same skeleton every time: `while queue` → snapshot `len(queue)` → pop that many, push children → then extract.
level order → res.append(level)
right side view → res.append(level[-1])
level averages → res.append(sum(level)/len(level))
max per level → res.append(max(level))
The queue preserves left→right order within a level (push left before right), so `level[-1]` is genuinely the rightmost node. Once you own the loop, this whole family is nearly free.

title: How do you treat an array as a linked list, and when does that create
front: How do you treat an array as a linked list, and when does that create a cycle?
back: Let the value be the next index: `i = nums[i]` (the array version of `curr = curr.next`). A duplicate value means two indices point to the same place — two predecessors for one node — which closes a loop. The cycle's entrance is the duplicate. Works because values are in `[1, n]` (always valid indices) and never 0 (so index 0 is outside the cycle — a safe start).

title: Binary search — two loop styles: `while l <= r` with `mid±1` vs `while
front: Binary search — two loop styles: `while l <= r` with `mid±1` vs `while l < r` with `r = mid`. When do you use each?
back: `l <= r`, `mid±1`, return l or r → searching for a value/boundary you can safely exclude mid from (classic search, insert position, Koko). `l < r`, `r = mid`, return nums[l] → converging ON a position when mid itself might be the answer (find min in rotated array, find peak) — you can't exclude mid on the "keep" side, so shrink to it, and the strict `<` stops the loop when pointers meet.

title: Sliding window — max/min of every window. Why can't a single running-m
front: Sliding window — max/min of every window. Why can't a single running-max variable work?
back: You can add to a max but you can't "un-max" — when the current max leaves the window, a lone variable doesn't know the next-largest. Use a monotonic deque: keep candidates in decreasing order, front = current max.

title: BFS — do you add to `visited` when you push a cell or when you pop it?
front: BFS — do you add to `visited` when you push a cell or when you pop it?
back: At push. Marking at pop lets the same cell be queued several times before it's processed — by different neighbours in the same level — which wastes work and can corrupt counts. Push and mark together, always.

title: Removing duplicates from a sorted array vs a sorted linked list — why
front: Removing duplicates from a sorted array vs a sorted linked list — why are the approaches completely different?
back: Array (LC26): contiguous memory, so deleting means shifting everything → instead write survivors forward with a slow pointer, return the count. Linked list (LC83): nothing moves — route around the duplicate with `curr.next = curr.next.next`, one arrow changes. No second pointer, no dummy (the head is the first occurrence of its value, so it never gets deleted). This is the whole reason linked lists exist: O(1) deletion vs an O(n) shift.

title: Complexity — a recursive function uses no arrays or dicts. Is it O(1)
front: Complexity — a recursive function uses no arrays or dicts. Is it O(1) space?
back: No — every paused recursive call sits on the call stack. Space = O(max depth). Tree DFS: O(h) (log n balanced, n skewed). This is memory even though you declared nothing.

title: You need to remove a whole run of equal nodes from a linked list. What
front: You need to remove a whole run of equal nodes from a linked list. What's the clean way?
back:
Don't unlink node by node. Walk to the end of the run, step one past, then repoint once:
python
while curr.next and curr.next.val == curr.val:
 curr = curr.next # last node of the run
curr = curr.next # first node after it
prev.next = curr # cut the whole run in ONE assignment
Guard `curr.next` before reading `.val` (`1→1` crashes otherwise). And if you rewire without advancing `curr`, it ends up sitting on a detached node and the outer loop corrupts everything downstream.

title: Grid DFS — when does `dfs` return something, and when nothing?
front: Grid DFS — when does `dfs` return something, and when nothing?
back:
Same distinction as trees.
EDITING → mutate, return nothing Islands (mark visited), Flood Fill (repaint)
MEASURING → capture the 4 returns, combine Max Area of Island
Measuring shape, and it's `maxDepth` with four children instead of two:
if <guard>: return 0 # base case
visited.add((r, c))
return 1 + dfs(r+1,c) + dfs(r-1,c) + dfs(r,c+1) + dfs(r,c-1)
tree: return 1 + max(L, R)
grid: return 1 + up + down + left + right
The bug to watch: writing the four calls but discarding their return values — every region then reports size 1.

title: Binary search on the answer — what problem shape signals it, and what
front: Binary search on the answer — what problem shape signals it, and what do you search over?
back: "Minimize (or maximize) some value subject to a constraint" — e.g. slowest eating speed that still finishes in h hours. You binary-search the range of candidate answers (speeds 1..max), using a check function "does this candidate satisfy the constraint?" as the yes/no signal. Works because the check is monotonic: once a speed works, all faster speeds work. Answer = first yes = `l`.

title: Does polymorphism require inheritance?
front: Does polymorphism require inheritance?
back:
No. `SpiderMan` and `BlackWidow` share no base class, yet one `battle_sequence(hero)` handles both — it just calls `.attack()` and works with whatever responds. Polymorphism needs a shared interface (common method names), not a shared ancestor. When they do appear together, inheritance is usually there to share code (`__init__`, `self.name`), not to enable the polymorphism.
inheritance → avoid duplicating code
polymorphism → different types answering the same call

title: With multiple inheritance, why isn't `super()` simply "my parent"?
front: With multiple inheritance, why isn't `super()` simply "my parent"?
back: It's "the next class in the MRO of the object you're actually working with." In `class D(B, C)` where both inherit from `A`: inside `B`'s method, `super()` goes to `C`, not `A` — because C is next in D's MRO. So the same `super()` call resolves differently depending on what was instantiated. That's the diamond problem, and it's why people say prefer composition over inheritance beyond one level: "has a" is easier to reason about than "is both."

title: What does a heap actually give you, and what does it not?

You can't ask for the median or the 3rd element without dismantling it. It's partially ordered, not sorted — full ordering would be more work than the question needs.

title: Python sets — what are they for, how do you create/use one, and what c
front: Python sets — what are they for, how do you create/use one, and what can't they do?
back: Store things, answer "have I seen this?" in O(1). Create: `set()` (empty — `{}` is a dict!) or `{1,2,3}` or `set(list)` to dedupe. Use: `s.add(x)` · `x in s` · `s.remove(x)` / `s.discard(x)` (no error if absent) · `len(s)`. Can't: index (`s[0]` fails), hold unhashable things (no lists inside). Unordered.

title: What does `super().__init__()` do?

title: Python — what is `__init__` and when does it run?
front: Python — what is `__init__` and when does it run?
back: The setup method. Python runs it automatically the moment you create an object — `Dog("Rex")` triggers it, `"Rex"` lands in its parameter. You never call it yourself. It does NOT create the object (Python makes the empty object first, then hands it in as `self` to be filled) and it must NOT return anything.

title: A tree helper returns depth, and you compare `L == R` at the parent to
front: A tree helper returns depth, and you compare `L == R` at the parent to test some property. When does this silently fail?
back: When depth doesn't determine the property. Equal depths ≠ equal shape: `[1,2,3,4,null,null,5]` has depth 2 on both sides but is lopsided and not perfect. Depth carries no shape information, so no comparison at the parent can recover it. Ask: what does the parent actually need to know, and does my return value carry it? If not, return more (a tuple) — don't try to infer it.

title: A problem says "repeatedly remove X until you can't." What structure d
front: A problem says "repeatedly remove X until you can't." What structure does that phrasing point to, and why?
back: A stack. "Repeatedly" means removals cascade — elements that weren't adjacent become adjacent once something between them vanishes (`"azxxzy"`: remove `xx` and the two `z`s meet). Index-based splicing can't survive that, since every removal invalidates your indices. A stack keeps the previous surviving element on top at all times, so the cascade resolves automatically with no re-scanning.

title: Border-seeded grid search — Pacific Atlantic and Surrounded Regions us
front: Border-seeded grid search — Pacific Atlantic and Surrounded Regions use the same inversion. What differs?
back:
The selection, not the search. Both seed from the border and mark what's reachable.
417 Pacific Atlantic → KEEP what the search reached (pcf & atl)
130 Surrounded Regions → FLIP what it did NOT reach
In 130 the rule is "a region survives iff it touches the border" — so mark everything border-connected as safe, then sweep and flip every remaining `'O'`. Three passes: seed from the four edges, mark, then flip the unmarked.

title: Tree problems split into two modes. What are they, and how does the co

Editing (mutate the tree): change the node, recurse, `return node` — e.g. invert swaps children then returns the node; the recursive calls' return values aren't needed because they mutate in place. title: Binary search — no exact match exists (e.g. floor of √x). What do `l`
front: Binary search — no exact match exists (e.g. floor of √x). What do `l` and `r` mean when the loop exits, and which do you return?

title: `sorted(people, key=lambda p: p[1])` — what does Python actually do wi
front: `sorted(people, key=lambda p: p[1])` — what does Python actually do with the key, and what comes back?
back:
It calls the key once per item, sorts by those results, and returns the original items reordered. The key values are only used for comparing; they never appear in the output.
("Anna", 30) → 30
("Bob", 25) → 25 sort by 25, 30, 35
("Cleo", 35) → 35 → [("Bob",25), ("Anna",30), ("Cleo",35)]

title: Python — a = a + b vs a += b on a list?

a += b mutates IN PLACE, exactly like a.extend(b), so inside a function it changes the caller's list.
For immutable types (int, str, tuple), += always makes a new object.

title: Your recursive helper returns a depth in one branch and `False`/`0`/a
front: Your recursive helper returns a depth in one branch and `False`/`0`/a tuple in another. Why is that dangerous?
back: Callers can't tell the cases apart, and Python won't complain. `False == 0` numerically, so a parent absorbs it as a real depth and the failure vanishes silently. A bare `0` where a tuple is expected crashes only later, somewhere else. Rule: one function, one return shape, on every path — including the base case. If you need two quantities, return a tuple everywhere or track the second one outside.

title: Why must set elements and dict keys be immutable?
front: Why must set elements and dict keys be immutable?
back: Sets/dicts store items by their hash, computed from the value. If the value could change, its hash would change and the item would sit in the wrong place, impossible to find. So only immutable (hashable) objects are allowed. A tuple counts only if all its contents are hashable: `(1, [2])` fails.

title: Python — break a string into words / into characters?

Words: `s.split()` (no arg = any whitespace; `s.split(",")` for a delimiter). Characters: `list(s)`. NOT `s.split("")` — errors.
Also: Python — glue a list of strings into one string? → `" ".join(words)` — the separator owns the method, the list goes inside. `"".join(...)` for no separator. Opposite of split.
Also: Python — trim whitespace from the ends of a string? → `s.strip()` (both ends), `.lstrip()` / `.rstrip()` (one end). Returns new.
Also: Python — swap part of a string? → `s.replace(old, new)` — all occurrences, substring-based, returns new.

title: Binary search on a rotated sorted array — what's the decision structur
front: Binary search on a rotated sorted array — what's the decision structure at each mid, and why can't one condition do it?
back: Two questions, in order: (1) which half is sorted? — test `nums[l] <= nums[mid]` (the `<=` matters: l can equal mid on 2-element ranges). (2) Is target in that sorted half's range? — range check with BOTH bounds, then go there or to the other half. One fused condition can't work because only a sorted half can be range-checked — the other half wraps. Key fact: after rotation, one half is always sorted.

title: You'd need a DFS/BFS from every cell to answer the question. What's th
front: You'd need a DFS/BFS from every cell to answer the question. What's the move?
back:
Invert it — start at the targets and search outward. Pacific Atlantic: instead of "from each cell, can water reach an ocean?", start at the ocean edges and walk uphill — those are the cells that could drain in. Walls and Gates: instead of "from each cell, how far to a treasure?", seed every treasure and BFS out. O(mn) instead of O((mn)²).
The reversal usually deletes machinery too — no per-cell reset, no flags, no "did I reach it?" check, because you're starting where the answer is.

title: Binary tree — pre-order vs in-order vs post-order: what's the differen
front: Binary tree — pre-order vs in-order vs post-order: what's the difference and when do you use each?
back: Where you act relative to the children. Pre = act before recursing → info flows DOWN (path tracking, passing a running total). In = left, act, right → on a BST this yields values in sorted order (kth smallest, validate BST). Post = recurse first, act after → results bubble UP. Post-order is the workhorse — it's the skeleton above.

title: `res.union(dish)` in a loop leaves `res` empty. Why, and what's the fi
front: `res.union(dish)` in a loop leaves `res` empty. Why, and what's the fix?
back:
`.union()` is a query — it returns a new set and doesn't touch `res`. The command version mutates in place: `res.update(dish)` (or `res |= dish`, or rebind with `res = res.union(dish)`).
QUERY (new set back) COMMAND (mutates, returns None)
a.union(b) a | b a.update(b) a |= b
a.intersection(b) a & b a.intersection_update(b) a &= b
a.difference(b) a - b a.difference_update(b) a -= b
Third family of this trap after `sorted`/`.sort()` and `reversed`/`.reverse()`.

title: Python — what's wrong with naming a variable `round`, `list`, or `type

back: It shadows the built-in — the real function becomes unreachable in that scope, and any later call to it (yours or a library's) breaks with a confusing error far from the cause. Common accidental ones: `list, dict, set, str, int, type, id, sum, min, max, next, input, round, filter, map`. Fix: qualify the name (`round_num`, `card_list`, `total_sum`). Editors usually color builtins differently — if your variable lights up, rename it.

title: "K largest / k smallest / top k" — what's the heap approach and why be

back: Keep a heap of size k. For k largest, use a min-heap: push each item, and pop when size exceeds k — the smallest keeps falling out, so the k largest survive. `heap[0]` is then the kth largest. O(n log k) vs sorting's O(n log n) — a big win when k ≪ n, and memory stays at k regardless of stream size. Shortcut: `heapq.nlargest(k, items)` / `nsmallest`.

title: Python — what is duck typing, and what's the trade-off?

Type hints are documentation, not enforcement. The cost: `Rock()` (no `.speak`) raises AttributeError at the moment of the call, with no warning beforehand. Java refuses to compile; Python finds out at runtime. `typing.Protocol` is the modern middle ground — declare "anything with speak()" without demanding a base class.

title: Python `heapq` — how do you create and use a heap?

title: You're given a class to implement with several methods. How do you dec
front: You're given a class to implement with several methods. How do you decide what goes in `__init__`?
back: Work backwards from what must survive between calls. Read each method and ask "what does it need to look up, and who put that there?" Every answer becomes an attribute. In Design Twitter: `follow` writes relationships that `getNewsFeed` reads → a follows structure. `postTweet` writes tweets the feed reads → a tweets structure. The feed needs ordering but there's no clock → a counter you control. That last one is the piece people miss: if you need time and none is given, invent it.

title: Deep-copying a graph recursively — why must you put the copy in the ma
front: Deep-copying a graph recursively — why must you put the copy in the map before recursing into neighbours?
back: A cycle points back at the node you're currently building. If it isn't in the map yet, the recursive call doesn't recognise it, builds a second copy, and recurses forever. Recording first means the cycle finds it mapped and returns immediately. The dict does double duty — original→copy translation and the visited set — which is why no separate `visited` is needed.

title: Why is a Stack data structure ideal for solving the Valid Parentheses

title: `@abstractmethod` on a method, but the class is still instantiable. Wh

With both, instantiating the parent, or a child that skips the method, raises TypeError at construction rather than failing later at the call site.

title: Python — `TypeError: speak() takes 0 positional arguments but 1 was gi
front: Python — `TypeError: speak() takes 0 positional arguments but 1 was given`, and you passed nothing. What happened?

title: Linked list reversal — the loop ends when `curr` is None. What do you
front: Linked list reversal — the loop ends when `curr` is None. What do you return, and why?
back: `return prev`. `prev` trails one step behind `curr`, so when curr falls off the end, prev stands on the last real node — the old tail = the new head. (Same idea as binary search's "return l": the loop's exit state carries the answer.)

title: After binary search finishes, what is `l`?
front: After binary search finishes, what is `l`?

title: What does it mean when a recursion removes something from a set on the
front: What does it mean when a recursion removes something from a set on the way out?
back:
Backtracking — undoing state as the stack unwinds, so the structure always reflects the current path rather than everything ever seen.
path.add(node)
for nxt in graph[node]: dfs(nxt)
path.remove(node) # ← no longer on the path
Contrast the grid pattern, where `visited.add()` is permanent because you only care whether you've been there. Add-and-remove is the signature of per-path state — the same reason Count Good Nodes passed context as a parameter instead of a shared structure.

title: Duck typing, ABC, or `typing.Protocol` — what's the trade-off?
front: Duck typing, ABC, or `typing.Protocol` — what's the trade-off?

title: What is a queue, and is it the same thing as a linked list?
front: What is a queue, and is it the same thing as a linked list?
back: A queue is an interface, not a structure — defined by one rule: FIFO, first in first out. Add at the back, remove from the front. A linked list is a structure (nodes holding references). A queue can be implemented with a linked list, an array, or a ring buffer — the queue is the behavior, the linked list is one way to build it. Analogy: "a line at a bakery" (rule) vs "people holding hands in a row" (arrangement).

title: Why is `visited` shared across all islands rather than reset per islan
front: Why is `visited` shared across all islands rather than reset per island?
back: If it reset, the outer loop would reach an already-flooded cell, see land, and count that island again. The set is one global "already accounted for" register; the counter is what distinguishes islands. It's also what terminates the recursion — two adjacent land cells always point at each other, so bounds checks alone can't stop the ping-pong.

back: Deleting needs the predecessor (`prev.next = prev.next.next`), not the target itself. `while fast` walks one step too far — slow lands on the node to delete. `while fast.next` stops one earlier, leaving slow before it. Rule: to delete, always land on the node before.

title: Queue and stack — the standard operation names, and what you actually

QUEUE (FIFO — a line)

STACK (LIFO — a pile)

title: Bayes — how do you derive it and use it (two boxes)?
front: Bayes — how do you derive it and use it (two boxes)?
back:
posterior = likelihood x prior / evidence.
P(A|B) = P(A and B) / P(B) (the condition shrinks your world).
- Top = likelihood x prior, P(B|A) P(A) = the path you care about.
- Bottom = evidence P(B) = all paths: P(B|A1)P(A1) + P(B|A2)P(A2).
Box 1 picked 80%, blue 30% vs 60%:

title: Probability — make a fair 50/50 decision from a biased coin (unknown p
front: Probability — make a fair 50/50 decision from a biased coin (unknown p)?
back:
Flip twice: HT -> "heads", TH -> "tails", HH or TT -> discard and repeat.
P(HT) = P(TH) = p(1-p) for ANY p, so the kept outcomes are exactly 50/50 (von Neumann trick).
Expected flips = 1/(p(1-p)); p = 0.4 -> keep a pair 48% of the time -> ~4.2 flips.

title: Binomial distribution: what is it, its MLE, and examples?
front: Binomial distribution: what is it, its MLE, and examples?
back:
Number of successes k in n independent tries, each with the same chance p.
Mean np, variance np(1−p).
MLE: p̂ = k/n.
Examples: 50 clicks out of 2,000 ad impressions (CTR 2.5%), frauds out of 10,000 transactions, conversions in one A/B arm.

title: C(n, k), n choose k: what does it count and how do you compute it by h
front: C(n, k), n choose k: what does it count and how do you compute it by hand?
back:
It counts the ways to choose k items out of n when order does not matter, e.g. which 3 of 6 games team A wins.
By hand: multiply k numbers counting down from n, then divide by k! (k factorial): C(6, 3) = (6 × 5 × 4) ÷ (3 × 2 × 1) = 120 ÷ 6 = 20. Why divide: 6 × 5 × 4 counts ordered picks (first win, second, third), and each set of 3 games appears in 3! = 6 orders.
Symmetry: C(n, k) = C(n, n − k), because choosing 3 winners = choosing 3 losers.
Anchors: C(n, 1) = n, C(n, 2) = n(n − 1) ÷ 2 (handshakes), C(4, 2) = 6, C(5, 2) = 10, C(6, 3) = 20, C(10, 2) = 45.
Used in the binomial formula: P(k successes in n tries) = C(n, k) × p^k × (1 − p)^(n − k).
Best of 7 goes to game 7 = 3–3 after 6: 20 × (½)^6 ≈ 31%.
Python: math.comb(6, 3).

title: Bootstrap vs cross-validation: what does each measure, and how?
front: Bootstrap vs cross-validation: what does each measure, and how?
back:
Bootstrap measures the uncertainty of a statistic: resample n rows with replacement, recompute the statistic (mean, median, AUC, a coefficient) many times, and the spread of the results is its SE (standard error) or CI (confidence interval).
It answers: how sure am I about this number?
CV (cross-validation) measures predictive performance: split the rows without replacement into k folds, train on k − 1, score on the held-out fold, and average.
It answers: how well will this model do on new data?
Neither replaces the other. A bootstrap does not give out-of-sample performance (training rows reappear), and CV does not give the uncertainty of a parameter.
Link: each bootstrap sample leaves out about 37% of the rows, which random forests use as out-of-bag data for a CV-like error estimate.

title: Bernoulli — everything in one card
front: Bernoulli — everything in one card
back:
Single yes/no trial, 1 or 0. Parameter p = P(1). Mean p, variance p(1-p), max variance 0.25 at p=0.5.
Shape: two bars, nothing between.
Use: one transaction is fraud or not. Sum n independent Bernoullis = Binomial (mean np, var np(1-p)).
Derivation trick: X is 0 or 1 so X^2 = X, so Var = p - p^2.
In ML: Bernoulli target -> logistic regression -> cross-entropy loss.

title: SD, SE, CI, PI — how do they chain together?
front: SD, SE, CI, PI — how do they chain together?
back:
SD = sqrt(variance).
SE = SD / sqrt(n).
CI = estimate +/- 1.96 x SE.
PI = estimate +/- 1.96 x sqrt(SE^2 + SD^2).
A/B difference: SE_diff = sqrt(SE_A^2 + SE_B^2).
Two ideas only:
(1) averaging n values divides the SD by sqrt(n);
(2) independent noises combine by ADDING VARIANCES, then one square root.
NAMES: SD = sigma (the TRUE spread of one observation) = s (the SD computed from your sample, the estimate you plug in). PI floor "+/- 1.96 sigma": as n grows SE -> 0, but sigma is a property of the data and never shrinks.

title: cdf vs inv_cdf in Python: how do the p-value and the critical value mi
front: cdf vs inv_cdf in Python: how do the p-value and the critical value mirror each other?
back:
- statistics.NormalDist().cdf(z) answers what share of the normal curve is to the left of z: cdf(1.96) = 0.975.
- statistics.NormalDist().inv_cdf(p) answers which z has share p to its left: inv_cdf(0.975) = 1.96.
They undo each other. p-value (you know your z statistic and want the tail area): p = 2 × (1 − NormalDist().cdf(|z|)), e.g. z = 1.96 gives a tail of 0.025, doubled = 0.05.
Critical value (you know the confidence and want the cut-off): z* = NormalDist().inv_cdf((1 + conf) ÷ 2), e.g. 95% leaves 2.5% in each tail, so 0.975 gives 1.96.
It is the same 1.96 read in opposite directions, which is why the 95% CI excludes 0 exactly when p < 0.05.

title: Poisson — when does it fit, mean and variance?

title: Sample size — what drives it up, and what is power?

title: Probability — how do you combine AND and OR (e.g. two dice show the sa
front: Probability — how do you combine AND and OR (e.g. two dice show the same number)?
back:
Recipe:
- list the WAYS to win;
- inside each way MULTIPLY (all its parts must happen);
- ADD across the ways (any one wins, they can't happen together).
Examples:
- Dice: ways 1-1, 2-2, ..., 6-6, each 1/6 x 1/6 -> 6 x 1/36 = 1/6.
- Same for guessing a card: 52 x (1/52 x 1/52) = 1/52.
- "The two things match" = the diagonal of the grid of all pairs.

title: p-value — explain it to a non-technical stakeholder, and what is the c
front: p-value — explain it to a non-technical stakeholder, and what is the classic slip?
back:
"It's a measure of surprise. We assume the change did nothing. The p-value asks: if that were true, how often would we see a difference this big from random variation alone? 0.0001 = about one in ten thousand, so 'it did nothing' is a poor explanation."
THE SLIP: "the chance it's random" flips it.
A p-value is P(data this extreme | no effect), NOT P(no effect | data).
Always start with "IF there were no real difference". The reverse claim would need the prior plausibility of the effect, which a p-value never looks at.

title: A/B test gives p = 0.30. Stakeholder says "it did nothing, kill it". R
front: A/B test gives p = 0.30. Stakeholder says "it did nothing, kill it". Response?
back:
Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. p=0.30 means we FAILED TO DETECT an effect, not that there is none.
Two different worlds give p=0.30: the change truly does nothing, OR it works but the test was underpowered.
The p-value cannot tell them apart.
Look at the CONFIDENCE INTERVAL: [-0.5%, +0.7%] rules out anything meaningful, so killing it is fair; [-4%, +12%] means underpowered and we learned nothing. Same p-value, opposite decisions.

title: Covariate balance — how do you check it, and what are the traps?
front: Covariate balance — how do you check it, and what are the traps?
back:
Compare groups on variables measured BEFORE the experiment: t-test for continuous, chi-square for categorical.
Traps: (1) ONLY pre-treatment covariates; anything measured after exposure could be changed by the treatment itself.
(2) MULTIPLE TESTING: 20 covariates at 0.05 -> ~1 flags by chance (64% chance of at least one). One flag at p=0.03 with SRM clean = probably chance. Check the size (standardised mean difference < 0.1 = fine) and adjust for it in the analysis (regression / CUPED). Stratified randomisation is the design fix for next time.

title: One-sided vs two-sided test: cut-offs, p-value, when to use each?
front: One-sided vs two-sided test: cut-offs, p-value, when to use each?
back:
Two-sided: a gap in either direction counts. H1 (alternative hypothesis): B ≠ A. Cut-off |z| > 1.96. p = 2 × (1 − Φ(|z|)), where Φ (phi) = share of the normal curve below a value.
One-sided: only the direction named in advance counts. H1: B > A. Cut-off z > 1.645. p = 1 − Φ(z). The same data can flip: z = 1.8 gives p = 0.072 two-sided vs 0.036 one-sided.
Default is two-sided, because you want to know if the change hurts.
One-sided only when the other direction cannot change the decision, decided in advance, e.g. a guardrail (did page load get slower?).
Trap: one-sided for better with z = −2.1 gives p = 0.98 and hides clear harm. Choosing one-sided after seeing the data = p-hacking. One-sided needs about 20% fewer users.

title: ML design — the data is huge (70B rows/year). How do you handle scale?
front: ML design — the data is huge (70B rows/year). How do you handle scale?
back:
Population != training set. Decompose the size into its factors (2M properties x 90 dates x 365 days) and SAMPLE THE BORING FACTOR: keep all positives and informative negatives, downsample near-duplicate negatives.
Training size is a sampling DECISION, not a constraint.
Catch: if the sampling rule depends on features, it biases the model -> reweight by inverse keep-probability and RECALIBRATE on an untouched holdout with the natural distribution. Never evaluate on the sampled set.

title: Confidence interval vs prediction interval — the difference in one lin
front: Confidence interval vs prediction interval — the difference in one line?
back:
A CI covers a PARAMETER (the mean, the rate), a PI covers ONE NEW OBSERVATION.
The CI carries estimation error only, so it shrinks toward zero as n grows.
The PI carries estimation error PLUS the natural scatter of individual points, so it is always wider and shrinks only to a floor of about +/-1.96 sigma.
Even with infinite data, one new observation still varies. That sigma is the same irreducible noise as in the bias-variance decomposition.

title: Poisson — shape (e.g. lambda = 3)?
front: Poisson — shape (e.g. lambda = 3)?
back: Discrete, never negative, right-skewed. lambda=3 peaks at 2 and 3 (~22% each), ~5% at 0, tail past 6. Bigger lambda = more symmetric, looks Normal.

title: PCA: how does it work, explained to a non-technical person?
front: PCA: how does it work, explained to a non-technical person?
back:
Plain version: many measurements tell overlapping stories. For hotels, price, stars, room size and review score all say roughly how upscale a hotel is.
PCA (principal component analysis) replaces them with a few summary scores that keep most of the information, like turning a 20-question survey into 2 or 3 scores.
Picture: photographing an object from the angle that shows the most detail.
Technical version: rotate the data onto new axes ordered by variance. The first component is the direction where the data spread out most, the next is the largest remaining spread at right angles to it (uncorrelated), and so on. Computed from the covariance matrix (its eigenvectors) or SVD (singular value decomposition). Standardise first, or big-scale features dominate. Keep enough components to explain about 90% of the variance.
Uses: compress correlated features, remove collinearity, plot in 2D.
Caveats: components are mixtures that are hard to explain, it only captures linear patterns, and it ignores the target, so the biggest spread is not always the most predictive.

title: Two cards from a deck: P(both aces)?
front: Two cards from a deck: P(both aces)?
back:
4/52 x 3/51 = 12/2652 = 1/221 = ~0.45%.
MULTIPLY (AND), and the second fraction changes because one ace and one card are gone.
Adding (13.6%) is wrong: "both aces" can't be more likely than "first card is an ace" (7.7%).

title: Bernoulli — derive variance p(1-p). The trick?
front: Bernoulli — derive variance p(1-p). The trick?
back: X is 0 or 1 so X^2 = X, so E[X^2] = p. Var = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2 = p - p^2 = p(1-p). Mean = p = share of 1s = the fraud rate.

title: Survivorship bias — what is it, fraud example?
front: Survivorship bias — what is it, fraud example?
back:
You only see what made it through a filter.
Fraud: studying the fraud that got past your rules shows only the fraudsters clever enough to beat your defences, not fraud as a whole. Or analysing only active accounts, ignoring customers who churned, maybe because of a false block.

title: MSE on binary labels — is it wrong? What actually goes wrong?
front: MSE on binary labels — is it wrong? What actually goes wrong?
back:
Not wrong: it pushes in the right direction and gets there eventually. Just slowly on confident mistakes.
Toy: fraud row, model starts at 1%, same learning rate. CE reaches 46% in 5 steps, 83% in 10. MSE is still at 1% after 10 steps, ~10% after 50, needs ~100 to catch up.
Why: at 1% the model sits on the FLAT end of the sigmoid, and MSE keeps that flatness in its gradient; CE cancels it (gradient = p - y).
Plus: CE is convex for logistic regression (MSE with sigmoid isn't) and is the Bernoulli likelihood, so its probabilities are meaningful.

title: Monitoring a model after deployment — what do you watch?
front: Monitoring a model after deployment — what do you watch?
back:
Five layers, "is it running?" to "is it making money?":
(1) SYSTEM: latency p99, errors, throughput (seconds).
(2) INPUT DATA: missing-value rates, feature PSI (minutes-hours).
(3) OUTPUT: score distribution, flag rate, 3DS share (hours).
(4) PERFORMANCE: recall at FPR, AUPRC, calibration, at the same label age (weeks).
(5) BUSINESS: EUR fraud loss, decline rate, complaints, analyst hit rate.
Always BY SEGMENT; fast label proxies (analyst confirmations, customer reports); random holdout for unbiased labels.
Retraining: scheduled (fraud always drifts) + triggered (PSI > 0.25, recall below floor); new model must beat the current one as a CHALLENGER.

title: iid: what does it mean, and why does it matter?
front: iid: what does it mean, and why does it matter?
back:
iid = independent and identically distributed.
Independent: each draw tells you nothing about the next one.
Identically distributed: every draw comes from the same distribution, with the same probabilities.
- iid: rolling the same fair die 10 times.
- Not independent: cards drawn without replacement (the deck changes), or sessions from the same user (same habits).
- Not identically distributed: summer vs winter bookings (different probabilities).
Why it matters: SD ÷ √n (standard error), the CLT (central limit theorem) and t-tests all assume iid. When it breaks, e.g. repeated users or time series, the SEs come out too small and p-values too optimistic.
Fixes: aggregate to one row per user, cluster the SEs by user, or bootstrap whole users instead of rows.

title: Type I vs Type II error: what's the 2×2?
front: Type I vs Type II error: what's the 2×2?
back:
H0 true + reject H0 → Type I error, false positive, rate α (alpha) = 5%.
H0 true + fail to reject → correct.
H0 false + reject → correct, power = 1 − β (beta) = 80%.
H0 false + fail to reject → Type II error, false negative, rate β = 20%.
Fraud: Type I = blocking a legit customer, Type II = missing a fraudster, power = recall.
