title: CI vs p-value — how are they related, and why report the CI?
front: CI vs p-value — how are they related, and why report the CI?
back:
Same statistic, two framings. Both come from the lift and its SE.
- z = lift / SE_diff counts how many SEs the lift is from zero.
- The p-value starts FROM ZERO: how surprising is this data if the true effect were zero? p = 2 x P(Z > |z|), two-tailed.
- The CI starts FROM THE ESTIMATE: which true effects are plausible? lift +/- 1.96 x SE.
They always agree: zero outside the 95% CI = |z| > 1.96 = p < 0.05 (1.96 is the z where the two tails sum to 0.05).
Example: 0.6 / 0.317 = z 1.89, p ~ 0.058, CI [-0.02, +1.22].
Report the CI because it also gives the SIZE and precision of the effect.
Mental map: z 2 -> p 0.05, z 2.6 -> 0.01, z 3 -> 0.003.
Caveat: proportion tests use a pooled SE, so at the edge they can differ slightly.
note: fold into card 129: same idea twice

title: Confidence interval — what is it, and what does the 95% actually refer
front: Confidence interval — what is it, and what does the 95% actually refer to?
back:
A range built from your sample to capture an unknown FIXED parameter (e.g. the true fraud rate), expressing the noise in your estimate. Width = estimate +/- 1.96 x SE for 95%; SE shrinks as 1/sqrt(n), so more data = tighter.
The 95% describes the PROCEDURE, not this interval: repeat the sampling and 95% of the intervals built would contain the truth. You CANNOT say "95% chance the truth is in this one" because the truth is fixed, not random. That claim belongs to a Bayesian credible interval.
note: fold into card 28: same idea twice

title: What does a 95% CI mean, and what are the wrong readings?
front: What does a 95% CI mean, and what are the wrong readings?
back:
CI (confidence interval) = estimate ± 1.96 × SE (standard error).
Meaning: if you repeated the sampling many times, about 95% of the intervals would contain the true value.
Client version: 'Our best estimate is +5%. We measured a sample, so a rerun would differ a bit. Allowing for that, the lift is between +1% and +9%, and the method captures the true effect 95 times out of 100.'
Picture: a net, and 95 of 100 nets catch the fish.
Link it to the decision: range includes 0 = can't rule out no effect, low end beats the cost = pays off even if pessimistic, very wide = need more data.
Wrong readings: '95% chance the true value is in this interval' (the true value is fixed, the interval varies) and '95% of the data lies inside' (that's the prediction interval, ± 1.96 × SD, the standard deviation).

title: Two fraud models: same AUPRC, A has much lower log loss. What's differ
front: Two fraud models: same AUPRC, A has much lower log loss. What's different, when do you care?
back:
Same AUPRC = same RANKING. Lower log loss = A is better CALIBRATED (B's probabilities are off, e.g. inflated by undersampling).
Only ranking/threshold (top-200 queue) -> no practical difference.
Score used as a PROBABILITY (p x amount, fixed cut-offs like "above 30% block", reporting risk) -> A is better. B is cheap to fix: recalibrate (Platt / isotonic) on a holdout with the natural class balance.

title: SQL — each call involves two people; count it for BOTH the caller's an
front: SQL — each call involves two people; count it for BOTH the caller's and the callee's country. How?
back:
Turn each call into one row per side: JOIN person p ON p.id IN (c.caller_id, c.callee_id).
Or explicitly: SELECT caller_id AS person_id, duration FROM calls UNION ALL SELECT callee_id, duration FROM calls.
Say the assumption out loud: a domestic call now counts twice for that country.
note: SQL; never a reason for a no

title: SQL — compare a group's aggregate with a global aggregate (e.g. countr
front: SQL — compare a group's aggregate with a global aggregate (e.g. country avg > overall avg). How, and what's the classic error?
back:
HAVING AVG(duration) > (SELECT AVG(duration) FROM calls), a scalar subquery.
Error: referencing a CTE column in HAVING (HAVING avg > a.glob_avg) when the CTE isn't in the FROM -> "unknown column".
A CTE is only visible where you select FROM it (or CROSS JOIN it). Compute the global value on the RAW table: on an exploded/joined table each row may be duplicated and the average shifts.
note: SQL; never a reason for a no

title: Fraud rate 2% has tiny variance (0.0196). Easy to estimate precisely?
front: Fraud rate 2% has tiny variance (0.0196). Easy to estimate precisely?
back: No. Relative error matters: SE = sqrt(p(1-p)/n). n=1000: ~3% of p at p=0.5 but ~22% of p at p=0.02. Rare events need much bigger samples (A/B tests on fraud/conversion).

title: Linear regression — linearity fails. Example, what breaks, fix?
front: Linear regression — linearity fails. Example, what breaks, fix?
back:
Fails when: y doesn't change in a straight line with x, e.g. spend grows with income, then flattens.
Shows as a CURVE in residuals vs fitted (systematically + in some places, - in others).
Breaks: predictions AND coefficients, the model is the wrong shape.
Fix: transform (log), add polynomial/interaction terms, or use trees.

title: How does the bootstrap get an SE from a single sample?
front: How does the bootstrap get an SE from a single sample?
back:
It runs the same simulation, but draws the repeated samples with replacement from your own sample.
SE ≈ SD of the resampled estimates.

title: Sample size — how do you get it by reversing the CI, and why 2.8 and n
front: Sample size — how do you get it by reversing the CI, and why 2.8 and not 1.96?
back:
Set the true lift (MDE) = 2.8 x SE_diff and solve for n, with SE_diff^2 = [pA(1-pA) + pB(1-pB)] / n.
Using 1.96 ("CI just clears zero") gives only 50% power: the observed lift lands below the true one half the time.
2.8 = 1.96 (significance) + 0.84 (80% power), about 2x the sample.
Fraud 0.20% vs 0.15%: 1.96 -> ~54k per group; 2.8 -> ~109k.

title: How do you get the SE of an estimate from a simulation?
front: How do you get the SE of an estimate from a simulation?
back:
Repeat the experiment many times and take the SD of the estimates, e.g. stdev of the 2,000 means.
SE = how much the estimate wobbles from sample to sample.
note: fold into card 34: same idea twice

title: Supervised vs unsupervised learning: what's the difference, with examp
front: Supervised vs unsupervised learning: what's the difference, with examples?
back:
Supervised learns a labelled target, where you know the right answer for past cases: a fraud classifier trained on labelled fraud, a demand forecast from past bookings.
Unsupervised has no labels and finds structure: segments (clustering customers into groups) and anomalies (cases unlike the rest, e.g. odd transactions).
Semi-supervised sits in between: a few labels plus lots of unlabelled data, useful when labels are scarce or biased, as in my KYC (know your customer) work, where only investigated cases get labels.
Evaluation differs: supervised uses held-out labels (accuracy, AUC = area under the ROC curve), unsupervised needs judgement or a downstream use.

title: SVM — what is it, when is it used?
front: SVM — what is it, when is it used?
back:
Finds the boundary with the MAXIMUM MARGIN between classes; only the nearest points (SUPPORT VECTORS) define it.
KERNELS (e.g. RBF) give non-linear boundaries without hand-built features.
Loss = hinge (only cares about being on the right side with margin) -> NO probabilities.
Pros: strong on small/medium high-dimensional data (text), robust margin.
Cons: training ~quadratic in rows, impractical for millions of transactions; no probabilities; needs scaling; tune kernel + C.
Largely replaced by GBMs on tabular data.

title: Bayes: name the four parts, and fill them in for the two boxes (box 1
front: Bayes: name the four parts, and fill them in for the two boxes (box 1 picked 80%, blue 30% in box 1 vs 60% in box 2).
back:
posterior = likelihood × prior / evidence
- Prior: P(A), P(box 1) = 0.8 : belief BEFORE the ball
- Likelihood: P(B|A), P(blue | box 1) = 0.3 : how well "box 1" explains blue
- Evidence: P(B), 0.8×0.3 + 0.2×0.6 = 0.36 : all paths to blue
- Posterior: P(A|B), 0.24 / 0.36 = 2/3 : belief AFTER the ball
80% → 67%: blue is evidence against box 1, but the strong prior keeps it ahead.
MLE (likelihood only) would pick box 2; the prior flips it.
note: fold into card 0: same idea twice

title: SQL — window frame variations: which ones, and what's each for?
front: SQL — window frame variations: which ones, and what's each for?
back:
Shape: {ROWS | RANGE} BETWEEN start AND end.
- UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW = running total.
- 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW = 7-row rolling window (counts ROWS, not days: missing dates stretch it; use RANGE over UNIX_DATE(date) for true days).
- 1 PRECEDING AND 1 FOLLOWING = centred moving average.
- CURRENT ROW AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING = remaining total.
- UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING = whole partition (share of total).
- Shorthand: only a start -> end = CURRENT ROW.
note: SQL; never a reason for a no

title: Poisson — everything in one card
front: Poisson — everything in one card
back:
Counts of events in a fixed window. Parameter lambda = rate. P(k) = lambda^k e^-lambda / k!. Mean = variance = lambda. Assumes events are independent, rate is constant, no two at the same instant.
Shape: discrete, never negative, right-skewed, more symmetric as lambda grows.
Use: fraud alerts per hour. It is the Binomial limit (n large, p small, np = lambda), which is WHY mean = variance: np(1-p) with p tiny. If observed variance >> mean, the data is overdispersed (events cluster, e.g. fraud rings), so use a Negative Binomial.

title: Central limit theorem — what is it and why does it matter practically?
front: Central limit theorem — what is it and why does it matter practically?
back:
Average n independent draws from ANY distribution with finite variance; as n grows, the distribution of that AVERAGE becomes Normal, centred on the true mean with spread sigma/sqrt(n).
Example: single transaction amounts are heavily skewed, but averages of 1,000 transactions form a bell curve.
Why it matters: it licenses z-tests, CIs and 1.96 in A/B tests even when the data isn't Normal. Each user's conversion is a 0/1 Bernoulli, but the RATE is an average, so it's ~Normal. You only need the mean and variance, not the full distribution.

title: Chi-square test: what business question does it answer?
front: Chi-square test: what business question does it answer?
back:
Is a difference in counts across categories real, or just chance?
It compares what you actually saw with what you would expect if nothing were going on. A gap bigger than chance usually produces means a real difference.
Business uses:
1. Do groups behave differently? Mobile vs desktop booking rates, or conversion in test vs control (same answer as the two-proportion z-test).
2. Is the experiment healthy? We planned a 50/50 split but got 50,600 vs 49,400 users. Chance would almost never do that (p ≈ 0.0002), so something is broken, e.g. a redirect failing for one arm, and the results cannot be trusted until it is fixed (SRM = sample ratio mismatch).
3. Did the mix change? E.g. the device mix of bookers from two marketing channels. What to say to a stakeholder: we compared the counts we saw with the counts we would expect if there were no difference, and the gap is too big to be chance.
Limits: it says there is a difference, not how big or which group drives it, so look at the table. Use counts of users (not percentages or sessions) and enough data in each cell.
Formula if asked: χ² = Σ (observed − expected)² ÷ expected, and for a 2×2 table it equals z², with cut-off 3.84 = 1.96².

title: SRM check by hand: 50,600 vs 49,400 users on a planned 50/50 split. Is
front: SRM check by hand: 50,600 vs 49,400 users on a planned 50/50 split. Is the split broken?
back:
Expected 50,000 per arm.
Each arm: (observed − expected)² ÷ expected = 600² ÷ 50,000 = 7.2,
so χ² (chi-square) = 7.2 + 7.2 = 14.4.
df (degrees of freedom) = 2 − 1 = 1, so the cut-off is 3.84 = 1.96².
14.4 is far above it, so yes, it is broken (z = √14.4 ≈ 3.8, p ≈ 0.0002).
Same with the z-test: share 0.506 vs 0.5, SE (standard error) = √(0.5 × 0.5 ÷ 100,000) ≈ 0.0016, z = 0.006 ÷ 0.0016 ≈ 3.8. Business check: chance moves a fair split by about √(n × 0.5 × 0.5) ≈ 160 users (one SD, standard deviation), so 600 off is almost 4 SDs. Flag at about ±310 users (1.96 × 160) for 5%, and many teams use a stricter bar such as p < 0.001. Action: do not trust the results until you find the cause (e.g. a redirect failing for one arm, or bot filtering).

title: Dice game: roll, win the face value, may reroll once (must take the re
front: Dice game: roll, win the face value, may reroll once (must take the reroll). Strategy and value?
back:
A fresh roll is worth (1+...+6)/6 = 3.5.
Keep if you beat 3.5: keep 4, 5, 6; reroll 1, 2, 3.
Value = average of (3.5, 3.5, 3.5, 4, 5, 6) = 25.5/6 = 4.25 (vs 3.5 without the option).
The reroll only replaces your bad rolls.
Two rerolls: fallback is now 4.25, so keep only 5 or 6 on the first roll.

title: Bias and variance — define both via the 100-training-sets thought expe
front: Bias and variance — define both via the 100-training-sets thought experiment
back:
Draw 100 training sets, train the same model on each, ask all 100 to predict one customer. You get 100 predictions.
BIAS = their mean minus the truth (off-centre, aiming wrong).
VARIANCE = their spread around their own mean (wobble when the data changes).
Bias and variance are just mean and variance applied to predictions, treating the training sample as the random thing.

title: Offline vs online metrics — what's the difference and why do they disa
front: Offline vs online metrics — what's the difference and why do they disagree?
back:
OFFLINE = on historical labelled data before deploy (AUPRC, recall at fixed FPR on a time split): does the model RANK well?
ONLINE = live, after deploy (EUR fraud loss, chargebacks, decline rate, 3DS rate, conversion, customer contacts): did the BUSINESS improve?
They diverge because: (1) offline can't see customer reactions (more 3DS -> abandoned payments), (2) label delay (chargebacks take 30-90 days), (3) feedback loop (blocked transactions never get labels), (4) fraudsters adapt, (5) training-serving skew, (6) distribution shift.

title: Log loss / cross-entropy — what is it and what does it evaluate?
front: Log loss / cross-entropy — what is it and what does it evaluate?
back:
Cross-entropy = log loss = negative log-likelihood: the average of -ln(probability given to what ACTUALLY happened). -(1/N) sum[y ln p + (1-y) ln(1-p)]; y is an on/off switch, one term per row.
Toy: fraud p=0.9 -> 0.11; legit p=0.99 -> 4.61 (one confident error = 70% of the total).
Evaluates BOTH ranking and calibration (AUC metrics only see ranking): halve every score -> AUPRC unchanged, log loss worse.
A PROPER scoring rule: minimised only by the true probabilities.
Imbalance trap: predicting 0.2% for everyone gives ~0.014, which looks great but is just the base rate; always compare to that baseline.
note: fold into card 54: same idea twice

title: Linear regression — normal errors fails. Example, what breaks, fix?
front: Linear regression — normal errors fails. Example, what breaks, fix?
back: Fails when: residuals aren't bell-shaped. E.g. spend is heavily right-skewed. Check with a Q-Q plot. Breaks: only small-sample tests and intervals; with large n the CLT covers it. Coefficients and predictions fine. Fix: log the target, bootstrap.

title: Python — [x] vs list(x) vs list[x]?
front: Python — [x] vs list(x) vs list[x]?
back:
[x] = BUILDS a list containing x -> [5].
list(x) = CONVERTS an iterable to a list: list("ab") -> ['a','b']; list(5) -> TypeError (int not iterable).
list[x] = a TYPE HINT (like list[int]), not a list; arr + list[x] -> TypeError "not types.GenericAlias".
To add one element: arr[:i] + [element]. Never name a variable "list": it overwrites the built-in.
note: duplicate of Python 222

title: In SE = SD/√n, what is n?
front: In SE = SD/√n, what is n?
back: The number of values in one sample (inside each average), not the number of simulation repeats. 100 values give 1/√100 = 0.1, however many repeats you run.

title: Mean vs variance — what does each answer and why do you need both?
front: Mean vs variance — what does each answer and why do you need both?
back:
Mean = where it sits on average. Variance = how much it swings around that. Two alert queues both average 50/day, std 5 vs 30: same mean, completely different staffing.
Mean = what to expect, variance = how much to trust it. ALWAYS square-root variance before judging size, it is in squared units (var 0.0009 = std 0.03, which is 75% of a 0.04 mean, not small).

title: Welch vs classic (Student's) t-test: which and why?
front: Welch vs classic (Student's) t-test: which and why?
back:
Classic pools both groups' SDs (standard deviations) into one and assumes they are equal.
Welch uses each group's own SD, so SE (standard error) of the gap = √(SE_A² + SE_B²).
Use Welch by default: same answer when the SDs are equal, safe when they are not. It matters most when group sizes and SDs both differ (with equal sizes both give the same t).
Coding trap: scipy.stats.ttest_ind runs the classic test unless equal_var=False.

title: Cross-entropy / log loss — the full answer in one card?
front: Cross-entropy / log loss — the full answer in one card?
back:
= negative log-likelihood of Bernoulli labels: L = -[y ln p + (1-y) ln(1-p)].
So minimising it IS maximum likelihood: "I use log loss because my labels are Bernoulli and that's their likelihood."
Why not MSE: MSE caps the confident-wrong penalty at 1 and its gradient vanishes there (p=0.01, y=1: CE gradient 0.99 vs MSE ~0.02); CE grows without bound. With a sigmoid the gradient is clean: dL/dz = p - y, dL/dw = (p - y)x (error x input). Convex for logistic regression.
Multiclass -> softmax cross-entropy.

title: Bernoulli — what is it, mean, variance?
front: Bernoulli — what is it, mean, variance?
back: Single yes/no trial, 1 or 0, P(1)=p. E.g. one transaction fraud or not. Mean p, variance p(1-p). Sum of n independent = Binomial.
note: fold into card 5: same idea twice

title: Significance level (alpha) — what is it?
front: Significance level (alpha) — what is it?
back:
The FALSE-ALARM rate you accept when nothing is really there, chosen BEFORE the test.
A/B test: of all changes that truly do nothing, alpha = 0.05 means 5% will still look like wins.
Fraud analogy (null = "customer is legit"): alpha = share of LEGIT customers you'd block (the FPR).
Reject the null when p < alpha. Confidence level = 1 - alpha (0.05 -> 95% CI). Pick it from the cost of a false alarm: stricter when it's costly or hard to undo.
note: fold into card 112: same idea twice

title: High variance — where does it actually show up, given training error i
front: High variance — where does it actually show up, given training error is near zero?
back: In the GAP between training and test error, not in training error. A depth-30 tree memorises each training set, so it is near-perfect on train and much worse on test. Retrain it on another sample and you get a different model making different mistakes. High variance means unreliable, not necessarily bad on every single test set.

title: How to calculate cross-entropy vs MSE for one binary row?
front: How to calculate cross-entropy vs MSE for one binary row?
back:
TRICK for CE: take the probability the model gave to the TRUE class, then -ln of it.
Fraud (y=1) with p = 0.8: true-class prob = 0.8 -> CE = -ln(0.8) = 0.22.
Legit (y=0) with p = 0.8: true-class prob = 1 - 0.8 = 0.2 -> CE = -ln(0.2) = 1.61.
MSE: squared distance to the label, (y - p)^2 -> fraud 0.04, legit 0.64.
Full formula CE = -[y ln p + (1-y) ln(1-p)]: y switches one term on.
Ranges: MSE 0 to 1 (capped), CE 0 to infinity.
Anchors: -ln(0.5) = 0.69, -ln(0.1) = 2.3, -ln(0.01) = 4.6.

title: A/B test — the CI is on WHAT, and how does it relate to the p-value?
front: A/B test — the CI is on WHAT, and how does it relate to the p-value?
back: On the DIFFERENCE between groups (the lift), not on each group's metric. Each group has its own CI, but the decision is about the effect, so the uncertainty must be about the effect. For a 95% CI, "the difference-CI excludes zero" is the SAME statement as p < 0.05. But the CI also gives the MAGNITUDE, which the p-value doesn't, so it's the better thing to show a stakeholder. Don't eyeball whether the two group CIs overlap; they can overlap while the difference is still significant.
note: fold into card 129: same idea twice

title: When a user-level A/B test breaks (interference), which designs do you
front: When a user-level A/B test breaks (interference), which designs do you use?
back:
User-level tests break when treated and control units affect each other (interference): shared supply in a marketplace, ad auctions and budgets, network effects, prices everyone sees.
Cluster randomisation: randomise groups (cities, hotels, friend circles) so interactions stay inside a group. Cost: fewer units, so less power, and SEs must be clustered.
Geo experiments: randomise regions, e.g. ads on in half the regions and off in the rest, often analysed with pre-period matching or synthetic control. Good for ads incrementality. Cost: few regions, spillover across borders.
Switchback: switch the whole market between treatment and control in random time slots (hours or days), for shared systems like pricing or auction settings. Cost: carryover between slots, so add washout periods.
Budget-split: in ad marketplaces, split each advertiser's budget into two halves, one per arm, so the arms do not compete for the same money. Holdout: keep a small group without the feature (or the ads) for weeks to measure the long-run effect.

title: Probability brain teasers — the 4-tool toolkit?
front: Probability brain teasers — the 4-tool toolkit?
back:
(1) COUNT PEOPLE, not probabilities: imagine 10,000 and fill a table (Bayes / base-rate). Each rate belongs to ONE column.
(2) AND MULTIPLIES: P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B given A); result gets SMALLER. OR adds minus overlap. Sanity: "both" can't beat "the first alone".
(3) "AT LEAST ONE" -> 1 - P(none). Never add probabilities (10 x 2% double-counts).
(4) EXPECTED VALUE = sum value x probability; for games, compare what you hold with the fallback; for waiting problems, call the answer E, condition on the first step (restart = E again), solve.

title: Sampling bias — what is it, fraud example?
front: Sampling bias — what is it, fraud example?
back:
Your sample differs from the target population because of HOW you collected it (a subtype of selection bias).
Fraud: training on transactions from established markets, then deploying in a new country where fraud and customer behaviour differ.

title: Sample size for an experiment — how do you determine it?
front: Sample size for an experiment — how do you determine it?
back:
Four inputs:
(1) alpha, usually 0.05 = tolerance for false positives.
(2) Power, usually 80% = chance of catching the effect if it's real.
(3) MDE, the smallest lift worth acting on = a BUSINESS decision.
(4) Variance of the metric from historical data; for a conversion rate it's p(1-p).
Per group n ~ 16 x variance / MDE^2 (at alpha 0.05, power 80%).
Then turn n into days of traffic, round up to full weeks, and fix it IN ADVANCE (no peeking).
note: fold into card 72: same idea twice

title: Log loss vs Gini / entropy impurity — what's the difference?
front: Log loss vs Gini / entropy impurity — what's the difference?
back:
IMPURITY describes a node's label mix.
LOG LOSS describes predictions against the truth.
Impurity: local, no predictions needed, used to pick SPLITS in a single tree / random forest (split = biggest impurity drop).
Log loss: global objective across the dataset, used to TRAIN gradient-based models and evaluate probabilities.
note: fold into card 109: same idea twice

title: Simpson's paradox for averages: how can every group rise while the tot
front: Simpson's paradox for averages: how can every group rise while the total falls?
back:
The pooled mean = w₁·m₁ + w₂·m₂ (w = each group's share, m = each group's mean).
If the shares shift towards the low group, the total can fall while every m rises.
Fix: split the change into within-group and mix parts, then ask why the mix moved. E.g. more cheap leisure bookings during a promotion.

title: Selection bias — what is it, fraud example?
front: Selection bias — what is it, fraud example?
back:
Whether a record gets into your data depends on something related to the outcome.
Fraud: SELECTIVE LABELS. You only learn if a transaction was fraud when you APPROVED it; declined ones never get a label, so training data is filtered by the previous model.
Fix: a small random holdout that is let through, to get unbiased labels.

title: z vs t: what's the difference and when do you use each?
front: z vs t: what's the difference and when do you use each?
back:
Same statistic: estimate ÷ SE (standard error) = how many SEs from 0.
The difference is how much you trust the SE.
- z: the SE is known exactly or n is large, so compare with the normal curve (1.96 two-sided, 1.645 one-sided).
- t: the SE uses the sample SD (standard deviation) from a small sample, so the SE itself wobbles. Compare with the t curve, which has fatter tails and a higher cut-off depending on df (degrees of freedom, n − 1 for one sample or for pairs): df 3 = 3.18, df 9 = 2.26, df 30 = 2.04, large = 1.96.
- Proportions use z (the SE comes from p itself and n is large).
Toy: 10 bookings, mean €108 vs €100, SD €12, SE 3.8, statistic 2.1. Significant against 1.96 but not against the t cut-off of 2.26. At Booking scale t = z.

title: Linear regression assumptions — how to rebuild the list from the equat
front: Linear regression assumptions — how to rebuild the list from the equation?
back:
Walk through y = b0 + b1x1 + ... + e.
THE SHAPE (b0 + b1x): is it really a straight line? -> Linearity.
THE X's: are the features distinct? -> No multicollinearity.
X AND e TOGETHER: is the noise unrelated to the features? -> Exogeneity.
THE e's, three questions about the noise:
- related to each other? -> Independence;
- same spread everywhere? -> Equal variance (homoscedasticity);
- bell-shaped? -> Normal errors.
One about the line, one about the x's, one about x and e, three about e. What breaks follows the same map: the e trio breaks only UNCERTAINTY (SEs, p-values); exogeneity breaks the COEFFICIENTS; linearity breaks EVERYTHING; multicollinearity breaks INTERPRETABILITY.
note: fold into card 114: same idea twice

title: Mean vs variance — what does each answer, why need both?
front: Mean vs variance — what does each answer, why need both?
back:
Mean = where on average.
Variance = how much it swings.
Two queues both avg 50 alerts/day, std 5 vs 30 = totally different staffing.
Mean = what to expect, variance = how much to trust it.
note: identical to card 52

title: Random variable — what is it, and discrete vs continuous?
front: Random variable — what is it, and discrete vs continuous?
back:
A random variable is a FUNCTION mapping outcomes to numbers, not "a random thing".
Discrete: countable values (fraud label 0/1, alerts per day, failed logins) -> described by a pmf.
Continuous: any value in a range (transaction amount, latency, model score) -> described by a pdf.
Bernoulli, Binomial and Poisson are discrete; the Normal is continuous.

title: Bias vs variance of a model, framed as mean and variance?
front: Bias vs variance of a model, framed as mean and variance?
back: A model is a random variable (depends on the training sample). Bias = is the MEAN prediction on the truth? Variance = SPREAD across retrains. Right on average doesn't help: you ship one model, not the average.
note: fold into card 46: same idea twice

title: Sample size — what's the formula, and what is it trying to guarantee?
front: Sample size — what's the formula, and what is it trying to guarantee?
back:
n per group ~ 16 x sigma^2 / MDE^2 (alpha 0.05 two-sided, power 80%).
sigma^2 = variance of one observation; for a rate, p(1-p).
GOAL: if the TRUE effect equals the MDE, an 80% chance the observed difference lands far enough from 0 that the CI excludes 0. The observed difference wobbles around the true one by ~1 SE, so put the true effect 2.8 SE from zero: 1.96 (significance bar) + 0.84 (room to wobble down and still clear it 80% of the time). Sizing so that "seeing exactly the MDE" just clears zero (1.96 only) gives 50% power.
Full form: 2.8^2 x 2 sigma^2 / MDE^2 ~ 15.7 sigma^2 / MDE^2; different rates: 2.8^2 x [pA(1-pA) + pB(1-pB)] / MDE^2.
Example: 5% baseline, +0.6pp -> ~21,000 per group.

title: Paired t-test: when, how, and why not Welch?
front: Paired t-test: when, how, and why not Welch?
back:
When the same units are measured twice (same hotels before and after, two fraud models on the same transactions).
Take one difference per unit, then t = mean difference ÷ SE(mean difference), where SE (standard error) = SD (standard deviation) of the differences ÷ √(number of pairs).
Why not Welch: one unit's two numbers are linked (a 20% hotel stays near 20%) and Welch ignores that link, so it counts the hotel-to-hotel spread as noise. Var (variance) of after − before = Var(after) + Var(before) − 2 × Cov (covariance), and Welch drops the Cov term.
Toy with 4 hotels and a 1-point gap: Welch t ≈ 0.2 vs paired t ≈ 5.

title: p-value — "so p=0.0001 means a 99.99% chance it works"?
front: p-value — "so p=0.0001 means a 99.99% chance it works"?
back:
No. A p-value is not the probability the hypothesis is true, and it says nothing about effect SIZE or importance.
A tiny p-value with a 0.1% lift is statistically significant and commercially pointless.
Statistical vs PRACTICAL significance. And 0.05 is a convention, not a law: it is the false-positive rate you are willing to accept, and should follow from the cost of being wrong.

title: Sigmoid — what is it?
front: Sigmoid — what is it?
back:
A converter from a score to a probability. The model adds up evidence into a score (any number); the sigmoid squashes it into 0-100%.
Score 0 -> 50% (no evidence either way).
Big positive -> near 100%, big negative -> near 0%, never reaching either.
SYMMETRIC: -score gives 100% minus the probability (+2.5 -> 92%, -2.5 -> 8%). Steep in the middle, flat at the ends (why MSE's gradient vanishes there).
Why THIS function: it makes the score = log-odds, so logistic regression weights are interpretable (weight 0.7 -> odds x e^0.7 ~ 2x).

title: What raises a test's power: the four levers?
front: What raises a test's power: the four levers?
back:
- More data n (SE = σ/√n shrinks)
- a bigger effect (bigger signal)
- less noise σ (cleaner metric, CUPED)
- a looser α (lower bar, but more false positives).
All four sit in n ≈ 16σ²/MDE² (σ = SD of the metric, MDE = minimum detectable effect, 16 from α = 5% and 80% power).
note: fold into card 81: same idea twice

title: For z/ t tests. Which SE goes in the denominator?
front: For z/ t tests. Which SE goes in the denominator?
back:
Ask how many estimated numbers are in the estimate.
- One estimate vs a fixed number: use that estimate's own SE.
- For a mean it is SD ÷ √n (is the average stay above 3 nights?).
- For a proportion it is √(p(1 − p) ÷ n), with p taken from H0 (SRM: share in arm A vs the planned 0.5).
- Two independent estimates: add their squared SEs, then take the square root: √(SE_A² + SE_B²).
- For two means (Welch), each group's SE = SD ÷ √n.
- For two conversion rates (A/B test), each group's SE = √(p(1 − p) ÷ n), with the pooled rate p under H0.
- Paired data is really one estimate (the mean difference vs 0), so it follows the first rule: SE = SD of the differences ÷ √(number of pairs).
Trap: SRM is not two groups, because the arms are two sides of one split (every extra user in A is one fewer in B), so there is only one random number. SE = standard error, SD = standard deviation, H0 = null hypothesis.

title: Drift detection — how, given fraud labels arrive 30-90 days late?
front: Drift detection — how, given fraud labels arrive 30-90 days late?
back:
Cheapest signal first:
(1) SCORE distribution (instant): did something change?
(2) FEATURE distributions (instant): what changed?
(3) PERFORMANCE once labels mature (AUPRC, recall at FPR, calibration): does it matter?
PSI = sum (actual - expected) x ln(actual/expected) over bins; < 0.1 stable, 0.1-0.25 watch, > 0.25 major.
Toy: 50/30/20 -> 40/30/30 = 0.06.
KS = biggest gap between two CDFs (with millions of rows everything is "significant", so PSI thresholds are more useful).
LIMIT: meaning drift can be invisible in inputs; only labels show it -> use fast proxies (analyst confirmations, customer reports, random holdout).

title: Variance vs standard deviation — what's the difference, and when do yo
front: Variance vs standard deviation — what's the difference, and when do you use each?
back:
Both measure spread around the mean.
VARIANCE = average SQUARED distance (squared units, e.g. alerts^2): squaring removes the signs, and variances ADD for independent things.
SD = sqrt(variance) = typical distance, in ORIGINAL units, so it's what you report.
Toy: 40, 50, 60 -> var 66.7, SD 8.2 alerts. SD 3 + SD 4 (independent) -> var 9 + 16 = 25 -> SD 5, NOT 7. Calculate with variances, communicate with SDs.

title: Sample Ratio Mismatch (SRM) — what is it and how do you check it?
front: Sample Ratio Mismatch (SRM) — what is it and how do you check it?
back:
Group sizes don't match the designed split.
50/50 of 100k, got 50,600 vs 49,400.
Count in A ~ Binomial(100k, 0.5):
- SD = sqrt(25,000) = 158, so 600 off = z ~ 3.8.
- Chi-square = sum (O - E)^2 / E = 7.2 + 7.2 = 14.4 = z^2; cutoff 3.84 = 1.96^2 -> p ~ 0.0002.
Same 50.6% split with 1,000 users -> chi-square 0.14, noise. SRM = something besides randomisation chose the groups -> don't trust the result.
note: fold into card 44: same idea twice

title: Power — what is it and what drives it?
front: Power — what is it and what drives it?
back:
The chance you DETECT an effect when it's really there (your catch rate; in fraud terms, like recall: of real frauds, how many you catch).
Power = 1 - beta; target 80%. It depends on effect / SE (signal vs wobble) and on the bar: bigger sample (smaller SE), bigger true effect, less noisy metric (CUPED) or a looser alpha all raise it.
Fraud example: a new rule truly cuts fraud 0.20% -> 0.15%. 54k per group = ~50% power (a coin flip); 109k per group = 80%.

title: Mean 50 EUR, sd 200, n = 1,000,000. CI for the mean is [49.6, 50.4]. S
front: Mean 50 EUR, sd 200, n = 1,000,000. CI for the mean is [49.6, 50.4]. So the next transaction is ~50?
back:
No, that confuses a parameter with an observation. SE = 200/sqrt(1e6) = 0.2, so the AVERAGE is pinned down tightly. But one transaction is a single draw with sigma = 200, so the prediction interval is ~50 +/- 1.96x200 = [-342, 442], a thousand times wider.
More data narrows what you know about the average and does nothing to make individual transactions less variable. (Negative lower bound = amounts are not Normal but right-skewed; use logs or quantiles.)

title: Fraud alerts average 3/hour. Variance of alerts per hour?
front: Fraud alerts average 3/hour. Variance of alerts per hour?
back: Can't tell from a rate alone, it only gives the mean. Need a distribution. If Poisson, variance = 3. Say "depends on the distribution we assume".
note: fold into card 41: same idea twice

title: Mean vs variance — what does each answer and why do you need both?
front: Mean vs variance — what does each answer and why do you need both?
back: Mean = where it sits on average. Variance = how much it swings around that. Two alert queues both average 50/day, std 5 vs 30: same mean, completely different staffing. Mean = what to expect, variance = how much to trust it. ALWAYS square-root variance before judging size, it is in squared units (var 0.0009 = std 0.03, which is 75% of a 0.04 mean, not small).
note: identical to card 52

title: Fitting linear vs logistic regression: what is optimised, and how is i
front: Fitting linear vs logistic regression: what is optimised, and how is it found?
back:
Two different things:
the rule (what you optimise) and the method (how you find it).
- Linear: rule = least squares (minimise squared errors), which equals MLE (maximum likelihood estimation) if the errors are normal. Method = closed form (normal equations), or gradient descent when the data are huge.
- Logistic: rule = MLE, which means minimising log loss (cross-entropy). Method = no closed form, so iterative: gradient descent or Newton's method.
MLE and gradient descent are not alternatives, they work together.
Interview line: logistic regression is fitted by maximum likelihood, i.e. minimising log loss, and solved iteratively because there is no closed form.

title: A/B test — calculate the CI on the difference in conversion rates
front: A/B test — calculate the CI on the difference in conversion rates
back:
Key step: variances ADD even for a difference, Var(A-B) = Var(A) + Var(B), for independent groups. Each rate is a Bernoulli mean, so SE = sqrt(p(1-p)/n). Therefore SE_diff = sqrt( pA(1-pA)/nA + pB(1-pB)/nB ), and CI = (pB - pA) +/- 1.96 x SE_diff.
Example: 500/10000 vs 560/10000 = 5.0% vs 5.6%, lift 0.6pp, SE_diff ~0.317pp, CI = [-0.02, +1.22]pp, contains zero, NOT significant (p ~ 0.058).

title: Probability — fair coin landed HHH. P(4th is heads)? And if fairness i
front: Probability — fair coin landed HHH. P(4th is heads)? And if fairness is uncertain?
back:
1/2: the 3 heads already HAPPENED (facts, not uncertain), and a coin has no memory.
0.0625 = P(HHHH) computed BEFORE any toss: a different question.
Streak thinking = GAMBLER'S FALLACY.
If fairness is uncertain, the heads are EVIDENCE -> Bayesian update.
Uniform prior (know nothing): Laplace's rule (heads + 1)/(tosses + 2) = 4/5 = 0.8.
Strong "coins are fair" prior: stays near 0.5. MLE would say 3/3 = 100% (overconfident, like 0 frauds in 50); Laplace = adding one imaginary head + one tail = smoothing.

title: Logistic regression — what is it, how is it fit, how do you read the c
front: Logistic regression — what is it, how is it fit, how do you read the coefficients?
back:
Linear regression on the LOG-ODDS, fitted by MLE.
Score z = b0 + b1x1 + ...; sigmoid turns it into p; loss = cross-entropy (Bernoulli NLL); no closed form -> gradient descent / Newton. Coefficient b = change in log-odds per unit; e^b = ODDS RATIO.
Fraud: new device b=0.7 -> odds x2; account age b=-0.5 -> odds x0.61 per year.
TRAP: it's the ODDS that change, not the probability ("cuts fraud probability by 39%" is wrong; at a 1% base rate doubling odds gives ~2%, at 50% gives 67%).
Assumptions: linearity in log-odds, independence, no multicollinearity, no perfect separation (-> regularise). No normal errors / equal variance needed.
Pros: interpretable, calibrated, fast, convex, strong baseline.
Cons: linear boundary, interactions must be hand-built, needs scaling.

title: Model performance dropped in production — how do you diagnose it?
front: Model performance dropped in production — how do you diagnose it?
back:
Four steps, cheapest first.
(1) IS IT REAL? Label maturity (chargebacks 30-90 days: compare at the SAME label age, e.g. recall known 14 days after the transaction), base-rate trap (precision down, recall + FPR stable = fraud got rarer), small numbers.
(2) IS IT THE SYSTEM? Empty/defaulted features, schema or unit change, broken join, new model version; confirm with a replay test + missing-value rates.
(3) IS IT THE WORLD? Input drift (feature PSI), fraud-rate drift, meaning drift (inputs normal, model wrong).
(4) WHERE? Slice by country, channel, merchant type, new vs old customers; drops are usually concentrated.
FIX follows cause: wait for labels / fix pipeline / recalibrate + threshold / retrain on recent data + new features; urgent new pattern -> temporary rule.
Toy: recall 70% -> 55%, all in card-not-present gift-card merchants = new fraud pattern.

title: Normal z-values to know by heart?
front: Normal z-values to know by heart?
back:
z = how many SDs a value sits from the mean: z = (x − μ)/σ, where μ (mu) = true mean and σ (sigma) = true SD.
For an estimate: z = (estimate − null value)/SE, where SE = standard error = SD of the estimate.
Two-sided:
- ±1 → 68%
- ±1.645 → 90%
- ±1.96 → 95%
- ±2.58 → 99%
- ±3 → 99.7%.
- One-sided: 1.645 → 95%, 0.84 → 80% (power).
- A two-sided 95% leaves 2.5% in each tail, so z = the 97.5% point = 1.96.
Python: statistics.NormalDist().inv_cdf(0.975).

title: Random forest vs XGBoost — "a random forest is trained on log loss, li
front: Random forest vs XGBoost — "a random forest is trained on log loss, like XGBoost." What's wrong?
back:
What's missing is a GLOBAL LOSS.
Random forest: each tree is grown greedily on IMPURITY reduction (make child nodes as clean as possible), independently, on its own bootstrap sample. The forest then just AVERAGES the trees, which optimises nothing and reduces VARIANCE. Nothing ever checks the forest's predictions against the truth.
XGBoost: trees built SEQUENTIALLY, each one fitted to reduce the whole ensemble's LOG LOSS via its gradients. Consequence: RF probabilities are often poorly calibrated; GBM's are closer, because only the GBM was pushed toward honest probabilities.

title: Type I vs Type II error — definitions, fraud framing, and link to A/B
front: Type I vs Type II error — definitions, fraud framing, and link to A/B testing?
back:
Null = "transaction is legit".
TYPE I = false positive = false alarm: blocked a good customer (rejected a true null).
TYPE II = false negative = miss: let fraud through (failed to reject a false null).
In an A/B test, Type I rate = alpha (0.05), Type II rate = beta = 1 - power (0.20).
For a fixed sample they trade off: lowering one raises the other. Only more data lowers both.

title: Expected coin flips to get two heads in a row (HH)?
front: Expected coin flips to get two heads in a row (HH)?
back:
Story:
- you need an H (2 flips on average), then 1 more flip;
- half the time it's T and you start over, which costs E again.
- E = 2 + 1 + 1/2 x E -> E = 6.
- The number in front of E = how often you start over (the failure rate).
Two sixes in a row: E = 6 + 1 + 5/6 x E -> E = 42.
General: E = 1/p^2 + 1/p. HT takes only 4: a wrong flip (H) doesn't lose your progress.

title: Severe class imbalance — how do you handle it?
front: Severe class imbalance — how do you handle it?
back:
In order:
(1) METRIC: accuracy is useless (all-legit = 99.8% at 0.2% fraud). Use PR-AUC or recall at a fixed false-positive rate; ROC-AUC can look great under imbalance. Time-based split.
(2) THRESHOLD from costs, often the whole fix: 0.5 is meaningless at a 0.2% base rate.
(3) Only if the model can't learn the minority: class weights or undersample the majority; be sceptical of oversampling/ SMOTE (rarely helps on tabular fraud, leaks if done before the split).
(4) Better FEATURES usually beat any rebalancing.
CATCH: weights and resampling distort probabilities (order is kept). Ranking/threshold only -> no calibration needed. Score used as a probability -> recalibrate: undersampling by k inflates odds by k. Model says 15% -> odds 0.176 / 10 = 0.0176 -> real ~1.7%.
note: fold into card 122: same idea twice

title: Variance of model scores — signal or noise?
front: Variance of model scores — signal or noise?
back:
Depends which spread.
ACROSS CUSTOMERS it is signal: a model scoring everyone 0.04 is not discriminating at all, you want spread.
ACROSS RETRAINS it is noise: that is model variance, the instability.
Same word, opposite reading.

title: Regression losses — MSE vs MAE vs Huber vs quantile vs Poisson, when e
front: Regression losses — MSE vs MAE vs Huber vs quantile vs Poisson, when each?
back:
MSE = MLE (max likelihood) under Normal noise; predicts the MEAN; big errors punished quadratically, so sensitive to outliers.
MAE = MLE under Laplace noise; predicts the MEDIAN; robust to outliers.
Huber = MSE for small errors, MAE for large ones: robust but smooth.
Quantile (pinball) loss = predicts a chosen quantile (e.g. P90 for "worst-case" transaction volume, prediction intervals). Poisson loss = counts per window (alerts per day), MLE for Poisson.

title: Linear regression — exogeneity fails. Example, what breaks, fix?
front: Linear regression — exogeneity fails. Example, what breaks, fix?
back:
Fails when: errors are related to the features, usually an omitted confounder.
E.g. an unmeasured trait (financial savviness) drives both income and spend. Breaks: coefficients are BIASED, even with infinite data; can't read them causally.
Fix: add the confounder, instrumental variables, or run an experiment.

title: ML design — how do you A/B test an ML model properly?
front: ML design — how do you A/B test an ML model properly?
back:
(1) Compare against the NAIVE alternative, not only "nothing": banner test = 3 arms (no badge / model badge / naive rule badge); the model's value = model vs naive.
(2) Randomisation unit = the level of INTERFERENCE (SUTVA): shared inventory -> cluster/property; one fraudster hits many transactions -> customer/card, not transaction.
(3) Primary read online (conversion, EUR loss); offline metrics only get you into the test.

title: pmf vs pdf vs CDF — what is each, and the classic trap?
front: pmf vs pdf vs CDF — what is each, and the classic trap?
back:
pmf = probability mass function, (discrete): actual probability at a point, P(X=2)=0.22, bars sum to 1.
pdf = probability density function, (continuous): DENSITY, not probability.
The trap: P(X = exact value) = 0 for a continuous variable, because there are infinitely many values.
Probability is the AREA under the curve over an interval, total area 1.
CDF (both): P(X <= x), runs 0 to 1, never decreases.
In practice you never ask "score = 0.4 exactly" (that is 0), you ask "score >= threshold", which is an area the CDF gives you.

title: Do mean and variance fully describe a distribution?
front: Do mean and variance fully describe a distribution?
back: Usually no, they summarize location and spread but not shape (skew, tails, discreteness). Poisson(4) vs Normal(4,4): same mean and var, different shape. Exception: the Normal is fully fixed by mu and sigma^2.

title: 20 metrics at α = 0.05: what goes wrong, and how do Bonferroni and BH
front: 20 metrics at α = 0.05: what goes wrong, and how do Bonferroni and BH fix it?
back:
Problem: each test has a 5% false-positive chance, so with 20 tests the chance of at least one false positive is 1 − 0.95^20 ≈ 64%, and about 1 metric wins by luck.
First fix is design: one primary metric chosen before the test.
Bonferroni: one strict threshold for every metric, α ÷ m (α = significance level, m = number of tests), here 0.05 ÷ 20 = 0.0025. It keeps the chance of any false positive (FWER, family-wise error rate) at 5% or below, but it is strict and misses real effects, especially with correlated metrics.
BH (Benjamini–Hochberg): a sliding threshold instead of the same small one. Sort the p-values from smallest to largest. The k-th smallest (k = rank) passes if p ≤ (k ÷ m) × 0.05, and everything up to the largest passing k is significant. It controls FDR (false discovery rate): on average at most 5% of the metrics you call significant are false. More power, so it is the usual choice for many metrics or segments.
Example (m = 20): p = 0.001, 0.004, 0.012 against thresholds 0.0025, 0.005, 0.0075 gives 2 significant with BH vs 1 with Bonferroni.

title: Disease 1%, test catches 99% of sick, 5% false positives. You test pos
front: Disease 1%, test catches 99% of sick, 5% false positives. You test positive: P(sick)?
back:
Count 10,000 people:
100 sick -> 99 test positive;
9,900 healthy -> 5% = 495 test positive.
You test positive: P(sick) = 99 / 594 = ~17%.
The low base rate makes false positives dominate. Same table as fraud precision and "share of A/B wins that are real".

title: Standard deviation vs standard error — what is the difference?
front: Standard deviation vs standard error — what is the difference?
back:
SD (sigma) = spread of the DATA, how much individual observations vary.
SE = spread of an ESTIMATE, how much your sample mean would move if you redrew the sample.
Connected by SE = sigma/sqrt(n).
So SE is just the standard deviation of a statistic.
Sigma is a fact about the world and does not change with n; the sqrt(n) is why more data tightens estimates.
For a proportion, sigma = sqrt(p(1-p)) from the Bernoulli, so SE = sqrt(p(1-p)/n).
CI uses SE (shrinks with n); prediction interval uses sigma (does not).

title: ML drift — the three types, in plain words?
front: ML drift — the three types, in plain words?
back:
"Covariate" just means FEATURE.
INPUT DRIFT (covariate / data drift): who shows up changes (new country, holiday spike); model often still fine.
FRAUD-RATE DRIFT (prior / label drift): how much fraud changes (ring shut down); ranking fine, precision and calibration off.
MEANING DRIFT (concept drift): what the signals mean changes (fraudsters adapt); model is WRONG -> retrain.
Fraud is full of meaning drift: adversaries adapt + blocked transactions never get labels.

title: t-test: what does it check and how is t built?
front: t-test: what does it check and how is t built?
back:
It checks whether two groups have the same true mean, not the same distribution.
t = estimate ÷ SE (standard error) of that estimate = gap between the means ÷ SE(gap) = how many SEs the gap is from 0.
Rule: |t| above about 2 (1.96) means p-value below 0.05.
Why t, not z: with few units the SD (standard deviation) estimate itself wobbles, so the cut-off is higher (3.18 with 4 pairs). At Booking scale t = z.
Trap: everyone spends €100 vs half €0 and half €200 gives the same mean, so t = 0 although the distributions differ. Testing for the same distribution = KS (Kolmogorov–Smirnov) test.

title: PM: "p = 0.03, so a 97% chance the feature works." Right?
front: PM: "p = 0.03, so a 97% chance the feature works." Right?
back:
No.
- p = P(result this extreme or more | no effect).
- The PM wants P(feature works | result), the flipped probability, which also depends on the prior (how often ideas work) and on power.
Same trap as reading a fraud screen's recall as precision. Say instead: strong evidence it's not luck, plus the lift and its CI.

title: What is a random variable?
front: What is a random variable?
back: A function mapping outcomes of a random experiment to numbers. Discrete = countable (alerts per month). Continuous = any value on a scale (transaction amount).
note: shorter copy of card 70

title: Poisson — why does variance equal mean?
front: Poisson — why does variance equal mean?
back: Slice the window into n pieces, each Bernoulli(lambda/n), so count = Binomial, var = np(1-p). n to infinity, p to 0, np = lambda, (1-p) to 1, so var = lambda.
note: fold into card 41: same idea twice

title: Impurity and log loss — how are they linked, and which models use whic
front: Impurity and log loss — how are they linked, and which models use which?
back:
If a leaf predicts its own fraud share q, its log loss EQUALS its entropy, so splitting on entropy = greedily minimising training log loss. Gini plays the same role for the Brier score (Gini = 2 x Brier).
Entropy <-> log loss, Gini <-> Brier.
Random forest / decision tree: split on Gini (default, faster) or entropy, similar splits in practice; no global loss is optimised.
XGBoost / LightGBM: NO impurity; each split is chosen by the reduction in the model's loss (gradient + hessian), so with binary:logistic, log loss drives even the splits.

title: Normal / Gaussian — everything in one card
front: Normal / Gaussian — everything in one card
back:
Continuous, parameters mu (mean) and sigma^2 (variance). Mean mu, variance sigma^2, and these two numbers fix it COMPLETELY (unlike other distributions, where shape needs more).
Shape: symmetric bell, unbounded both ways, 68 / 95 / 99.7 percent within 1 / 2 / 3 sigma. Standardise with z = (x - mu)/sigma to get Normal(0,1).
Why it is everywhere: the CLT, so sample means and sums of many small effects are approximately Normal regardless of the underlying distribution.
Use: measurement errors, model residuals, any average.
In ML: Normal errors -> MSE loss. Binomial goes Normal when np and n(1-p) are both above ~10.

title: Chi-square vs t-test — when do you use which?
front: Chi-square vs t-test — when do you use which?
back:
t-test: compares MEANS of a CONTINUOUS variable between two groups (past spend, account age).
Chi-square: compares COUNTS / PROPORTIONS of a CATEGORICAL variable.
Two forms: goodness-of-fit (observed vs expected counts, e.g. SRM) and test of independence (is the category distribution the same across groups, e.g. country by arm).
Rule: numbers you average -> t-test; things you count -> chi-square. (More than 2 groups, continuous -> ANOVA.)

title: Significance level vs p-value — the difference, and the classic misuse
front: Significance level vs p-value — the difference, and the classic misuse?
back:
alpha = the BAR, set BEFORE the test (how many false alarms you'll tolerate).
p-value = how surprising your data is if nothing is going on, computed AFTER.
Rule: p < alpha -> reject the null.
Misuse: p = 0.07, so you lower the bar to alpha = 0.10 "so it's significant". That's moving the bar after the jump (p-hacking): you can make anything significant, and the false-alarm rate is no longer controlled.

title: A/B test not significant — can I just collect more data until it is?
front: A/B test not significant — can I just collect more data until it is?
back:
No, that is PEEKING and it inflates the false-positive rate well above 5%: keep looking and stop the moment it crosses 0.05, and noise alone will eventually hand you a "significant" result. The lift itself doesn't change with more data; only your ability to distinguish it from zero does (4x the sample halves the SE).
The legitimate version: fix the sample size IN ADVANCE from the smallest lift worth detecting, run to it, look once. Sequential testing lets you peek properly, but adjusts the thresholds to pay for it.

title: Linear regression — what are the assumptions, and what does each break
front: Linear regression — what are the assumptions, and what does each break?
back:
(1) Linearity,
(2) Exogeneity: errors unrelated to the features,
(3) Independent errors,
(4) Homoscedasticity: constant noise spread,
(5) Normal errors,
(6) No multicollinearity.
What each breaks:
PREDICTIONS -> linearity.
COEFFICIENTS biased -> exogeneity (matters for causal claims).
Only UNCERTAINTY (SEs, p-values) -> independence, homoscedasticity, normality.
INTERPRETABILITY -> multicollinearity.
So for pure prediction most barely matter; for inference they all do. Check: residuals vs fitted (curve / funnel), Q-Q plot, VIF.

title: Python — res = arr1: copy or alias? When does it matter?
front: Python — res = arr1: copy or alias? When does it matter?
back:
ALIAS: two names, ONE list.
Mutating res (res.append, res.remove, res[0] = x) also changes arr1.
Rebinding res to a new list (res = res[:i] + res[i+1:]) doesn't, because slicing builds a new list.
Plan to mutate? Copy first: res = arr1.copy() (or arr1[:]).

title: Python — arr[:i] + element raises TypeError. Why, and how do you inser
front: Python — arr[:i] + element raises TypeError. Why, and how do you insert?
back:
+ on a list joins two LISTS; a single value isn't a list -> TypeError "can only concatenate list (not int) to list".
Wrap it: arr[:i] + [element].
Insert at i: arr[:i] + [element] + arr[i:] (new list, original unchanged) or arr.insert(i, element) (mutates, returns None, so never assign it).
Strings work without brackets because a character is itself a string: s[:i] + "x" + s[i:].

title: F1 — why a harmonic mean, and when to use it?
front: F1 — why a harmonic mean, and when to use it?
back:
F1 = 2PR/(P+R) = 2TP/(2TP+FP+FN).
Harmonic mean is dragged down by the SMALLER value, so you can't game it by maxing one side: flag-everything has recall 100%, precision 0.05% -> arithmetic mean ~50%, F1 ~0.1%.
TN doesn't appear, which is why it's sane under imbalance. It's a POINT metric at one threshold.
Use only when forced to one number with roughly symmetric costs; otherwise F-beta (F2 = recall 4x) or expected cost. Rarely right in fraud.

title: Same hotels before and after a change: what can a paired test not fix?
front: Same hotels before and after a change: what can a paired test not fix?
back:
Time. Pairing removes hotel-to-hotel differences, but if November differs anyway (season, holidays) every hotel moves without the badge.
Fix: give the badge to a random half of the hotels and compare their before→after change with the other half's (difference-in-differences).

title: ML design — how do you define the training row?
front: ML design — how do you define the training row?
back:
Template: "One row is ___ per ___; features from the trailing ___ window, frozen at the anchor; label = ___ within ___ after the anchor."
Banner: property x stay-dates, daily snapshot; features as-of snapshot; label = sold out within 48h.
Fraud: transaction at authorisation time; features from history before it; label = chargeback/confirmed fraud within 90 days.
Freezing features at the anchor prevents LEAKAGE.

title: Bias-variance trade-off — how does model complexity move each?
front: Bias-variance trade-off — how does model complexity move each?
back:
Simple model: high bias (too rigid), low variance (barely notices which sample it got) = UNDERFIT = stubborn.
Complex model: low bias (flexible), high variance (chases noise in this sample) = OVERFIT = jumpy.
Total error is U-shaped in complexity; validation finds the bottom.

title: Maximum likelihood (MLE) — what is it, and why do I care?
front: Maximum likelihood (MLE) — what is it, and why do I care?
back:
A rule for choosing parameters: pick the ones that make the observed data MOST PROBABLE. Write the likelihood, take the log (products -> sums, same maximum), maximise.
Bernoulli: 2 frauds in 10 -> p-hat = k/n = 0.2. Not an approximation: the MODEL is the approximation, MLE is the criterion.
Why care: every loss is MLE in disguise.
Bernoulli labels -> log loss; Normal noise -> MSE (least squares IS MLE); Laplace -> MAE.
"I use log loss because my labels are Bernoulli and that's their likelihood."
Catch: overfits small samples (0 frauds in 50 -> p-hat = 0) -> smooth or add a prior (MAP = regularisation).

title: Fraud-style class imbalance (e.g. 0.1% fraud): what goes wrong and wha
front: Fraud-style class imbalance (e.g. 0.1% fraud): what goes wrong and what do you do?
back:
Problem: accuracy is useless, because always predicting not-fraud scores 99.9%.
Metrics: PR-AUC (area under the precision-recall curve), plus precision and recall at the chosen threshold. ROC-AUC (area under the ROC curve) looks flattering when negatives dominate.
Training: class weights (missing a fraud costs more), or resampling (undersample legit, oversample fraud, e.g. SMOTE = synthetic minority oversampling), on the training data only, never the test set.
Resampling distorts the predicted probabilities, so re-calibrate afterwards.
Threshold: not 0.5. Set it by investigation capacity (e.g. analysts can review 200 alerts a day) and costs (a missed fraud vs a false alert).
Unseen patterns: add anomaly detection for new fraud types.

title: SQL — first N characters of a string?
front: SQL — first N characters of a string?
back:
LEFT(col, 3) or SUBSTRING(col, 1, 3); BigQuery: SUBSTR(col, 1, 3).
Positions start at 1, not 0 (Python: s[:3]).
Shorter strings return as-is, NULL stays NULL.
Last N: RIGHT(col, 3), BigQuery SUBSTR(col, -3).
Typical use: join or group on a prefix (country code, postcode area).
note: SQL one-liner; SQL was never a reason

title: ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC — imbalanced vs balanced?
front: ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC — imbalanced vs balanced?
back:
ROC on imbalanced: FPR's denominator is ALL negatives, so FPR 0.16% vs 0.32% looks identical on the curve but means 1,600 vs 3,200 false alarms (precision 20% -> 11%). Also averages over FPRs you'd never use. ROC-AUC 0.98 can coexist with 5% precision.
PR on balanced: works but worse, because (1) random baseline = prevalence, so values aren't comparable across datasets, (2) ignores TN, half the story when both errors matter, (3) ASYMMETRIC: swap the positive class and PR-AUC changes, ROC-AUC doesn't. ROC-AUC = P(random positive scored above random negative), 0.5 = random, base-rate independent.

title: Probability — Box A (20 pink + 20 white) vs Box B (40 + 40), draw 2 wi
front: Probability — Box A (20 pink + 20 white) vs Box B (40 + 40), draw 2 without replacement: which gives a higher chance of the same colour?
back:
Same colour = pink-pink OR white-white, so ADD both cases (here equal, so double):
A = 2 x 20/40 x 19/39 = 19/39 = 0.487;
B = 2 x 40/80 x 39/79 = 39/79 = 0.494 -> BOX B.
Intuition: the first ball uses up one of its colour; that penalty shrinks as the box grows, so P climbs toward 1/2 (= with replacement).
Shortcut: n of each colour -> (n-1)/(2n-1).
CHECK: list all outcomes (PP, PW, WP, WW); they must sum to 1. Forgetting WW gives 0.244, impossible for a 50/50 box.

title: Probability — when do you go forward and when do you flip to 1 - P(opp
front: Probability — when do you go forward and when do you flip to 1 - P(opposite)?
back:
Count the ways on each side, pick the side with FEWER ways.
- Flip when you see "at least one / any / not all" (the opposite, "none", is one single AND), or when your forward cases can OVERLAP (adding would double-count).
- Go forward for "exactly / all / both / none" with cases that can't overlap.
Example: At least one six in 4 rolls: 1 - (5/6)^4 = 0.52. Lift, all different floors: forward chain 4/4 x 3/4 x 2/4 x 1/4.

title: Logistic regression coefficient of 0.7: how do you interpret it, and h
front: Logistic regression coefficient of 0.7: how do you interpret it, and how do you turn it into a probability?
back:
The coefficient is the change in log-odds (the log of the odds), holding everything else fixed.
Say it as an odds ratio: e^0.7 ≈ 2, so the odds double.
Odds = cancel vs not cancel, not a share: 30% = 3 to 7.
Double the odds: 6 to 7, so the probability = 6 ÷ 13 ≈ 46%, not 60%.
Doubling the probability is the trap, and from 60% it would give an impossible 120%.
The probability change depends on the baseline: 10% becomes about 18%, 50% becomes about 67%.
Shortcut: for rare outcomes odds ≈ probability, so 2% becomes about 4%.
Interview line: free cancellation multiplies the odds of cancelling by about 2, holding the rest fixed.
Caveat: not causal, because unsure travellers choose free cancellation (an omitted variable), so you need an experiment.

title: When is it OK to bootstrap, and when not?
front: When is it OK to bootstrap, and when not?
back:
- OK:
- to estimate the SE or CI of a statistic with no simple formula (median, p95, ratios like revenue per booking, difference in medians, AUC), and for clustered data (resample whole users).
- Resample with replacement, the same size as your real sample n.
- Not OK:
- to increase the sample size or shrink the SE, because resampling bigger than n gives fake precision.
- Not needed:
- for the mean, where SE = s/√n (s = sample SD) gives the same answer.

title: t-test vs CI vs p-value: how do they relate, and which do you report?
front: t-test vs CI vs p-value: how do they relate, and which do you report?
back:
Same two numbers, the estimate and its SE (standard error), read three ways.
CI (confidence interval) = estimate ± 1.96 × SE: how big and how sure.
t = estimate ÷ SE: how many SEs from 0.
p-value: how surprising if there is no real effect.
They always agree: |t| above 1.96 ⇔ p below 0.05 ⇔ the 95% CI excludes 0.
Example: gap €5 with SE 2.5 gives t = 2, p ≈ 0.046, CI €0.1 to €9.9.
Report the effect with its CI (it also shows the size) and use the test for the yes/no.

title: Design an A/B test for a new feature: what are the steps?
front: Design an A/B test for a new feature: what are the steps?
back:
1. Hypothesis: what the feature should change and why (e.g. autoplay previews raise watch time).
2. Randomisation unit: the user, not the session, so each person sees one version and sessions are not double-counted.
3. One primary metric decided in advance (e.g. watch time per user), plus guardrails that must not get worse (crashes, latency, unsubscribes).
4. MDE (minimum detectable effect) and sample size: n ≈ 16σ² ÷ MDE² per arm, σ = SD (standard deviation) of the metric per user.
5. Duration: full weeks to cover weekday and weekend patterns, and long enough for novelty to fade.
6. Sanity checks: SRM (sample ratio mismatch: a chi-square test that the split really is 50/50) and an A/A test showing the setup finds no difference.
7. Pre-registered analysis: test, metric and outlier handling fixed before looking, and no peeking.
8. Decision rule: ship if the primary metric wins and no guardrail is hurt.
9. Ramp-up: 1% → 10% → 50% → 100%, watching the guardrails at each step.

title: Linear regression — multicollinearity. Example, what breaks, fix?
front: Linear regression — multicollinearity. Example, what breaks, fix?
back: Fails when: features are near-copies of each other. E.g. income and salary both in the model. Check with VIF (above ~5-10 = flag). Breaks: coefficients UNSTABLE and unreadable (large SEs, signs can flip). Predictions still fine. Fix: drop one, combine them, or L2 regularisation (ridge).

title: Naive Bayes: how does it score a case, and what goes wrong?
front: Naive Bayes: how does it score a case, and what goes wrong?
back:
Bayes' theorem plus the naive assumption that features are independent within each class, so their evidence just multiplies.
Toy (fraud):
- base rate 1%,
- new device in 60% of fraud vs 10% of legit,
- foreign merchant in 50% vs 20%.
- Fraud score = 0.01 × 0.6 × 0.5 = 0.003.
- Legit score = 0.99 × 0.1 × 0.2 = 0.0198.
- Chance of fraud given both = 0.003 ÷ (0.003 + 0.0198) ≈ 13%.
Each signal multiplies the odds: new device ×6 (60 vs 10), foreign merchant ×2.5 (50 vs 20).
What goes wrong: correlated signals are counted twice. If travelling legit customers show both signals 6% of the time instead of 2%, the true chance is ≈ 5%, so the model is overconfident even when its ranking is fine. Good for speed, little data and many features (the classic spam filter). Rarely right for fraud, where signals are correlated.

title: Base-rate trap — precision or PR-AUC changes between periods; did the
front: Base-rate trap — precision or PR-AUC changes between periods; did the model change?
back:
Precision and PR-AUC depend on the base rate; recall and FPR don't.
Same model (80% recall, 0.16% FPR) on 1M: Q1 0.4% fraud -> TP 3,200, FP ~1,594, precision 67%.
Q3 0.1% -> TP 800, FP ~1,598, precision 33%.
Same model, precision halved. DIAGNOSE a precision drop with recall unchanged: FPR stable = fraud got rarer (model fine); FPR rising = legit started looking suspicious (drift, model worse).
COMPARE models: score both on the SAME test set; across periods use ROC-AUC or PR-AUC / prevalence.

title: When is a model ready to ship?
front: When is a model ready to ship?
back:
"Better where it matters, safe where it could hurt, reversible if wrong."
(1) Beats the current model on the primary metric on the most RECENT untouched period.
(2) No leakage, no training-serving skew.
(3) Guardrails hold (decline rate, segment FPR, latency).
(4) NO SEGMENT WORSE (also the fairness check).
(5) Calibrated if used as a probability.
(6) Shadow mode passes.
(7) A/B or gradual ramp (1% -> 10% -> 100%) with monitoring + ROLLBACK plan ready.
(8) Documentation / model-risk sign-off. Overall +5% but new customers -10%? Net EUR per segment (new customers carry lots of fraud); route: new model where it wins, current one for new customers; fix why (reliance on history features).

title: Confusion matrix — precision, recall, FPR, and why accuracy fails (fra
front: Confusion matrix — precision, recall, FPR, and why accuracy fails (fraud toy)?
back:
1M transactions, 500 fraud, model flags 2,000, catches 400.
TP 400, FN 100, FP 1,600, TN 997,900.
Recall = TP/(TP+FN) = 80% (of frauds, how many caught).
Precision = TP/(TP+FP) = 20% (of alarms, how many real).
FPR = FP/(FP+TN) = 0.16% (of legit, how many bothered). Accuracy 99.83%, but all-legit scores 99.95%, HIGHER.
Tiny FPR next to 20% precision = the whole ROC vs PR story.

title: Confounding bias — what is it, fraud example?
front: Confounding bias — what is it, fraud example?
back:
A third variable drives both the treatment and the outcome, creating a fake association.
Fraud: "2FA users have 60% less fraud, so push 2FA." But customers who opt in are more careful and have older accounts, which lowers fraud on its own. Part of the gap is WHO chooses 2FA. Fix: randomise, or adjust for the confounders.

title: Linear regression — independence fails. Example, what breaks, fix?
front: Linear regression — independence fails. Example, what breaks, fix?
back:
Fails when: errors are related to each other. E.g. many rows per customer, or monthly data where one month predicts the next.
Breaks: standard errors too SMALL -> overconfident p-values and CIs. Coefficients still fine. Fix: clustered standard errors (by customer), time-series models.

title: L1 vs L2 regularisation — what does each do, and when to use which?
front: L1 vs L2 regularisation — what does each do, and when to use which?
back:
Both add lambda x penalty to the loss (a bias-variance dial).
L2 (Ridge) = sum of w^2: shrinks all weights smoothly, rarely to exactly zero; the default; handles CORRELATED features well by spreading weight across them.
L1 (Lasso) = sum of |w|: drives weights to EXACTLY zero, so it does feature selection; use when many features and few matter, or you need interpretability.
With correlated features L1 picks one arbitrarily and is unstable across samples.
Many AND correlated features (e.g. velocity over 1h/3h/6h) -> Elastic Net (L1 + L2).

title: Standard deviation vs standard error — what is the difference?
front: Standard deviation vs standard error — what is the difference?
back:
SD (sigma) = spread of the DATA: how much individual observations vary.
SE = spread of an ESTIMATE: how much your sample mean would move if you redrew the sample.
SE = SD / sqrt(n), so SE is just the SD of a statistic. Sigma is a fact about the world and doesn't shrink with n; SE does, which is why more data gives tighter estimates.
For a rate, sigma = sqrt(p(1-p)) from the Bernoulli, so SE = sqrt(p(1-p)/n).
Confidence interval uses SE (shrinks with n); prediction interval uses sigma (doesn't).

title: What is CUPED and why does it work?
front: What is CUPED and why does it work?
back:
Variance reduction with pre-test data: Y_cuped = Y − θ·(X − mean X), where Y = the metric during the test, X = the same user's metric before the test, θ (theta) = cov(X,Y)/var(X), the regression slope.
It removes the part history predicts (Anna spends a lot every month), so the mean stays the same but the noise drops.
Variance shrinks by (1 − ρ²), ρ (rho) = correlation of X and Y: ρ = 0.7 ≈ half the users for the same power.
Unbiased because X is measured before randomisation.
Catch: new users have no history.

title: Linear regression — homoscedasticity fails. Example, what breaks, fix?
front: Linear regression — homoscedasticity fails. Example, what breaks, fix?
back: Fails when: noise spread changes with the fitted value. E.g. high earners' spend varies much more than low earners'. Shows as a FUNNEL in residuals vs fitted (centred on zero, but widening). Breaks: standard errors wrong (usually too optimistic); coefficients STILL UNBIASED. Fix: robust (heteroscedasticity-consistent) SEs, or log the target.

title: Why do mean and variance matter in practice?
front: Why do mean and variance matter in practice?
back:
- Decisions (expected loss vs risk).
- Inference (CLT needs only mean+var, SE = sigma/sqrt(n) gives CIs, p-values, A/B sizing).
- Diagnostics (Poisson mean=var check).
- ML (bias-variance = mean and spread of model predictions).

title: SQL — UNION vs UNION ALL: what's the difference, and which is the defa
front: SQL — UNION vs UNION ALL: what's the difference, and which is the default choice?
back:
UNION = UNION ALL + remove duplicate rows (across the whole result, even duplicates within one input).
- UNION ALL keeps every row and is faster (no dedup step). Default to UNION ALL;
- use UNION only when you WANT distinct rows.
Trap: dedup silently breaks counts and sums when duplicates are legitimate (a player winning two slams in the same year -> two identical rows).
Both need the same number of columns with compatible types; names come from the first SELECT.
note: SQL; never a reason for a no

title: Gradient descent — what is it, and why does logistic regression need i
front: Gradient descent — what is it, and why does logistic regression need it?
back:
Walking downhill in fog: feel the slope where you stand, step downhill, repeat until the ground is flat (the minimum).
Height = error, position = the weights; every weight (knob) gets nudged at once.
Step size = steepness x learning rate: too small crawls, too big overshoots or diverges.
Each row "votes" on each knob with strength = how wrong the model was x the feature value; the knob settles where the votes balance.
Not like Bayesian HP tuning: GD KNOWS the direction from the slope and tunes weights inside one run; HP tuning guesses across full runs.
Logistic regression needs it because the weights are trapped inside the sigmoid, so "slope = 0" can't be solved with algebra (linear regression can: normal equations).

title: Decision tree — how does it work, and why does depth cause overfitting
front: Decision tree — how does it work, and why does depth cause overfitting?
back:
Asks yes/no questions: at each node it picks the feature + cut that gives the biggest IMPURITY drop (Gini/entropy); each leaf predicts its class share. No distributional assumptions, no scaling, captures interactions automatically.
DEPTH -> OVERFITTING: each level shrinks the groups (1M rows: depth 10 -> ~1,000 per leaf, depth 20 -> ~1 per leaf), so deep leaves fit a handful of rows and their NOISE = high variance.
Shallow = high bias (stubborn), deep = high variance (jumpy).
Controls: min samples per leaf (the REAL control; 1M rows, min 500 -> max 2,000 leaves, ~depth 11, so max depth 20 never kicks in), max depth (just a cap), pruning, or averaging trees (random forest).
For rare fraud, leaves must be big enough to hold positives (500 rows at 0.2% = ~1 fraud).
Pros: interpretable, non-linear, no scaling.
Cons: high variance alone, step-shaped predictions, greedy, poorly calibrated.

title: When an A/B test is impossible, what are the alternatives and their ke
front: When an A/B test is impossible, what are the alternatives and their key assumptions?
back:
Difference-in-differences: compare the before-after change in treated vs untreated groups (a feature launched in Spain only vs similar markets). Assumption: parallel trends, checked on the pre-period.
Synthetic control: build a weighted mix of untreated units that tracks the treated one before the change (a country with a TV campaign), and the gap after = the effect. For one or a few treated units.
Causal Impact (Google): forecasts the counterfactual time series from control series and the pre-period (Bayesian structural time series), and the gap = the effect.
Regression discontinuity: a cutoff decides treatment (a loyalty tier at 5 bookings), so compare just above vs just below. Assumption: nothing else jumps at the cutoff.
Instrumental variable: something that shifts treatment as if at random and affects the outcome only through it.
Matching or propensity scores: compare treated and untreated users who look alike on observed data. Assumption: no unobserved confounders, the hardest one to defend.

title: Bernoulli — where is variance largest, max value, why?
front: Bernoulli — where is variance largest, max value, why?
back:
p = 0.5, variance 0.25. 50/50 = most unpredictable.
Symmetric: p and 1-p give the same variance. Same reason entropy/Gini peak at 50/50.
