title: Non-parametric test vs bootstrap vs permutation test: when do you use
front: Non-parametric test vs bootstrap vs permutation test: when do you use each?
back:
Non-parametric (rank-based) tests: Mann–Whitney U for two independent groups, Wilcoxon signed-rank for pairs. Use them for small samples, outliers or ordinal data (ratings). Catch: they compare ranks (does one group tend to score higher), not means, so for revenue totals they answer a different question.
Bootstrap: resample the data with replacement to get the SE (standard error) or CI (confidence interval) of any statistic without an easy formula: median, p95, a ratio metric, a difference in medians, AUC. Resample users, not sessions, if rows are clustered.
Permutation test: a p-value by simulation. If H0 (no effect) is true, group labels do not matter, so shuffle the labels many times, recompute the difference each time, and p = the share of shuffled differences at least as extreme as the real one. Works for any statistic, with no distribution assumptions.
Rule: need a p-value without assumptions = permutation, need a CI for an awkward statistic = bootstrap, small or ordinal data and a standard test = rank-based.
Example: revenue per user with big spenders: a permutation test or a bootstrap CI on the difference in means, because Mann–Whitney would only say whether typical users spend more.

title: kNN vs k-means — the difference?
front: kNN vs k-means — the difference?
back:
kNN = SUPERVISED: predicts a label for a new point from its k nearest LABELLED neighbours (4 of 5 neighbours fraud -> 80%). No training (lazy), slow at prediction. k = neighbours that vote (small k overfits, large k underfits).
K-means = UNSUPERVISED: finds k groups in UNLABELLED data (assign points to nearest centre, move centres to the mean, repeat). k = number of clusters (pick via elbow / silhouette). Use: segmentation, or anomaly detection (far from every centre = unusual; with no labels, that's your only option of the two).
SHARED: both use distance -> both need FEATURE SCALING (euros swamp a 0/1 flag) and struggle in high dimensions.

title: Which features matter most for predicting an outcome, and how do you f
front: Which features matter most for predicting an outcome, and how do you find out?
back:
Clarify first: important for prediction, or a causal driver? Importance is not causation.
Model-agnostic: permutation importance on held-out data: shuffle one feature, which breaks its link to the target, and the drop in the metric is its importance (no retraining).
SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations): for each prediction, start from the average prediction and split the gap between it and this prediction among the features, giving each the average of its contribution over all orders of adding features, so the parts add up exactly.
Toy: average fraud score 2%, this case 30%, split as new device +15, foreign merchant +10, amount +5, account age −2.
Global importance = average absolute SHAP value.
Model-specific: standardised coefficients (linear or logistic), or tree gain and split counts (biased towards features with many distinct values).
Watch out: correlated features split or swap importance between them, so check stability across CV (cross-validation) folds, and use drop-column importance (refit without the feature) if you can afford it.

title: "At least one": 10 transactions, each 2% fraud independently. P(at lea
front: "At least one": 10 transactions, each 2% fraud independently. P(at least one fraud)? And the birthday problem?
back:
1 - P(none) = 1 - 0.98^10 = 1 - 0.817 = ~18% (not 10 x 2%, which double-counts).
BIRTHDAY, 23 people: P(all different) = 365/365 x 364/365 x ... x 343/365 = 0.493 -> ~50.7% share.
Why so high: 23 x 22 / 2 = 253 PAIRS. Mental shortcut: (364/365)^253 ~ e^(-253/365) ~ 0.5.

title: A/A test — what is it and why run one?
front: A/A test — what is it and why run one?
back: Run the experiment pipeline with NO difference between arms, before the real test. Any significant result or SRM means the pipeline itself is broken (assignment, logging, metrics), not the product. Also shows the real false-positive rate: at alpha 0.05, about 5% of A/A tests should come out significant; many more means something is wrong.
